blocks.h: CONTAINED, MOSTLY, THE FIRE SAID
Roya Publication No. 102
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

For forty-five years the Kamali family has lived in a glass house on a steel frame, high in the hills above Pacific Palisades. Parviz, an engineer who came from Tehran in 1976 and never went back, built it to stand a hundred years. His widow Āzar still teaches piano at its window. Their son Omid, who makes fake explosions sound real for a living, has moved back in with his wife and daughter to keep the house in the family.

Down the canyon, Captain Ray Maddox has spent twenty-seven years learning that a fire is never really put out. It is only stopped. His father fought the great Bel Air fire of 1961 and never quite stopped shaking.

It is the last winter of 2024. It has not rained in eight months, and the brush on the ridges has not burned in fifty years. The insurance letters came in the spring, to half the street at once. A pleasant man with a good watch has been knocking on doors, asking who might like to sell.

On New Year’s night, a small fire breaks out on the ridge above the Highlands, and the firefighters put it out before dawn. Then they are told to roll up their hoses and go home. The ground is still warm. The white flowers on the ridge, which only bloom in summer, are open in January.
And in the gaps between the chapters, something much older than the houses has started to talk.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book is fiction wrapped around something that happened.

The Palisades fire began on the morning of January 7, 2025, on a ridge above the Palisades Highlands, and burned for more than three weeks. It destroyed nearly seven thousand buildings and killed twelve people. Another fire, in Altadena, began the same evening and killed more. I have tried to keep the order of events, the weather and the broad shape of what went wrong faithful to the public record: the two wet winters and the eight dry months, the wind the forecasters warned about in words they almost never use, the engines that were not sent ahead of it, the shift that went home, the hydrants that ran dry in the high streets, the reservoir that had sat empty for a year, the gridlock on the one road out, the insurers who had left the hills the spring before, and the buyers who came for the burned land afterward. Because this is a story and not a report, I have kept its numbers loose on purpose. The fire’s own interludes carry the history.

On the cause. Federal investigators concluded that the Palisades fire was a holdover: the rekindling of a small fire set just after midnight on New Year’s Day, which smouldered underground in the roots of the brush for six days until the wind brought it back. Later reporting, and firefighters’ own sworn testimony, described crews being ordered to leave that first burn while the ground was still hot. A man was charged with setting the New Year’s fire. At the time this book was written, his first trial had ended with the jury unable to agree, and he was awaiting a second. He is not in this book, and nothing in it should be read as saying he did or did not do what he is accused of.

Everyone in this book is invented. The Kamalis, Ray Maddox, the chief in the clean jacket, the man with the good watch, the adjuster from Arizona and the landscaper whose name Omid finally learns are all made up. Real officials appear only by their titles, the Mayor and the Governor, and what they do here is only what was publicly reported. No insurer is named.

The suspicions in this book belong to its characters. The observations underneath them are real: the letters that came to so many houses in the same season, the lawsuits that followed claiming the insurers acted together, the empty reservoir and the state’s finding that a full one would not have saved the high streets, the report that was softened before it was published, and the offers made for land while it was still burning. I have tried to set the plausible beside the absurd and let the reader sort them, as Tara does on her mirror.

The datura is my invention. Sacred datura is a real Southern California wildflower, and the Chumash, who lived on that coast long before any of us, did use it to see what was coming. But no one has ever said that it bloomed on that ridge in January. That is the one thing in this book I have bent on purpose. Everything else was lying in plain sight.

The hills above the Palisades are built to burn. The only question they have ever asked us is how: in small fires we choose, in the cool months, with somebody watching, or in one enormous fire that chooses us.
Chew Z

Between the chapters of this story, someone else will speak. They are older than the houses, and older than the people who built the houses, and older than the names of the hills the houses stand on. They have been in your kitchen. They have been in your fireplace, and in the candle on your birthday cake, and in the small blue crown under your coffee every morning of your life. They are warm to the touch. Listen to them the way you would listen to a witness who has no reason left to lie.
I. THE HILLS ARE WAITING
1. Brush That Is Waiting Omid

My name is Omid Kamali [oh-MEED kaa-maa-LEE]. My father built our house because of a hill nobody wanted, and I lost it because of the same hill, and in between my family lived forty-five years on a slope that was always going to burn. Everybody knew it. The hill knew it best.

The hills above Pacific Palisades are covered in something called chaparral [SHAP-uh-RAL]. It’s a Spanish word, and it means, roughly, the kind of brush a man on a horse can’t get through. Scrub oak, sage, sumac, a hard little bush called chamise [shuh-MEEZ] that grows so tight you could stand a child on top of it. From the road it looks like green velvet thrown over the ridges. Up close it is sticks and oil and patience. Chaparral waits. It waits twenty years, thirty years, sometimes more. Then it needs to burn, the way a man who has been holding his breath needs to let it out.
Nobody told the hills about the property values.

My father’s name was Parviz [par-VEEZ]. He came from Tehran [teh-RAAN] in the autumn of 1976 with my mother, two suitcases, a degree in structural engineering and a letter from a firm in Century City that had promised him a year. A structural engineer is a person who makes sure buildings stand up. My father believed, with a faith I never saw him give to God, that anything could be made to stand up if you did the arithmetic honestly. He and my mother meant to stay three years. Then 1979 happened back home, and the country they had left turned into a country they could not go back to, and three years became the rest of their lives.
They were not sad about it, or if they were, they did it in Persian, where I couldn’t follow.

In 1979, the same year their old country closed behind them, my father bought a lot on a hillside in the Palisades Highlands. The Highlands is the high part of the Palisades, up a long road called Palisades Drive that climbs away from the ocean into the canyons. In those days it was new, raw, half-built. The lot was cheap because it was steep, and because the man selling it had watched the ridge above it burn once and said he’d rather live somewhere flat and boring for the rest of his life. My father told that story at dinner parties for forty years, as a joke about Americans. “He was afraid of a little fire,” my father would say, and the guests would laugh, and my mother would not.

My father designed the house himself. Steel frame, concrete footings sunk into the hillside like the roots of a tooth, and glass across the whole back, so that from the kitchen you looked down the canyon, past the rooftops of the village, to the Pacific Ocean. On a clear winter day you could see Catalina Island floating out there like something left behind by a better civilization. He used to stand at the glass with his coffee and say, “A hundred years. This house will stand a hundred years.” Then he’d knock on the steel column by the stairs, twice, the way other men knock on wood.

My mother, Āzar [aa-ZAR], taught piano. For forty years children came up that hill every afternoon to sit at her Steinway and be told, in a patient voice with a Tehran accent, that they were rushing. Some of their grandparents had once told her, in slower English than they used with each other, that she spoke very well. She taught their grandchildren anyway. My mother believes that revenge is a thing you do by outliving people and teaching their descendants to play Chopin properly.
Her name means fire. I didn’t think about that once in forty-six years. I think about it now.

I was born in Santa Monica in 1978, which makes me the first Kamali in several hundred years to be born near an ocean. I grew up in that glass house. I learned to ride a bicycle on its driveway, broke my wrist on its steps, kissed a girl for the first time on its back deck and was caught by my mother through the glass, which is the problem with glass. I went away to college, and came back, and went away to a marriage in Silver Lake, and came back again. I make sound for movie trailers. That’s my job. When you hear a building explode in a trailer and it sounds bigger than any building has ever sounded, that’s me, or people like me. I have spent twenty years making fake fire sound real.
I will leave you to decide how funny that is.

My father died in the spring of 2024, in April, of his heart, in his chair, looking at the ocean. He was eighty-one. He did not suffer, the doctor said, and I have chosen to believe the doctor, because it’s the kind of thing you only get to believe once.

After the funeral my wife and I talked about it for about a week, and then we did the thing everyone does and nobody plans. We rented out our place on the east side and moved into the house on the hill, with our daughter, Tara [TAA-raa], who was fifteen and furious about it for exactly one month, until she discovered that the view from her new bedroom was better than anyone’s at school. We told each other we were doing it so my mother wouldn’t be alone. That was true. It was also true that the house was mine now, on paper, and that some part of me wanted to stand at the glass with a coffee and knock on the column twice.

So that is who we were, in the last winter. Three generations in a house built to stand a hundred years, on a hill that had been waiting, by my later arithmetic, since roughly the Carter administration.
I should tell you about the weather, because the weather is the first character in this story and the only one who never lied.

The two winters before had been wet. Wet the way Southern California almost never is: storm after storm rolling in off the Pacific, the canyons running brown with water, the hills going so green in spring that people pulled over on the Pacific Coast Highway to photograph them. The grass came up waist-high. The mustard came up yellow. Everything that could grow, grew. We all said how beautiful it was, and it was.
Then the rain stopped.

It stopped in the spring of 2024, around the time we buried my father, and it did not come back. Not in the summer, which is normal. Not in the autumn, which is not. Not in October or November or December. By Christmas it had been eight months with almost nothing falling from the sky, and all of that beautiful waist-high grass had turned the colour of a paper bag, and all the new growth on the brush had dried to kindling where it stood. Kindling is the small stuff you use to start a fire, the twigs and paper under the logs. The hills above our house had become a very large fireplace, laid and ready, with nobody on duty to say whether it should be lit.

The scientists have a name for this. They call it whiplash: very wet, then very dry, one after the other, so the land grows a feast and then bakes it. I learned the word later, in a hotel room, from a television. At the time I only noticed that the hills had gone gold, and that my mother had stopped opening the back doors in the afternoon.
“Too dry,” she said, when I asked. “It smells like August.”
It was December. I told her she was imagining it.
I have been a sound engineer for twenty years, which means I have been paid to listen for twenty years. I didn’t hear a thing.
2. Mop-Up Ray
Twenty-seven years on the job and I have never once put out a fire.

I want to be precise, because nobody else in this story will be. Firefighters do not put out fires the way you put out a cigarette. We take things away from them. We take away their fuel, by cutting a line through the brush down to bare dirt, so there is nothing on the other side to eat. We take away their heat, with water, which soaks up heat faster than almost anything on earth. We take away their air, with dirt, with foam, with wet blankets on a kitchen pan. A fire is three things holding hands, fuel and heat and air, and all we ever do is break the grip. When the grip breaks, the fire isn’t dead. It’s just stopped. You learn that difference in your first year, and if you’re lucky you learn it by watching it go wrong on somebody else’s watch.

My name is Ray Maddox. I’m a captain in the city fire department, which is a smaller job than it sounds. It means I ride in the right-hand seat of an engine and make decisions I will later explain to people who were not there. I’ve been at the same station in the Palisades for the last eleven years, a low brick building near the bottom of the canyon with a flagpole and a basketball hoop and a kitchen where men with forearms like hams argue about chili. Before that I was all over the city. Before that I was a kid from the San Fernando Valley whose father had also been a firefighter, and whose father’s hands shook a little when he held a coffee cup, from something that happened in November of 1961 in Bel Air that he told me about exactly once.
I’ll tell you about 1961 some other time. Or someone will.

The part of the job nobody puts on a recruiting poster is called mop-up. After the flames are down and the television trucks have gone home, after the helicopter has flown back to wherever helicopters sleep, you walk the black. That’s what we call a burn area: the black. You walk it in a line, with hand tools, with a hose if you’re lucky, and you look for heat. You dig out stumps. You turn over logs. You crumble the ash in your fist. The old men taught me to take my glove off and hold the back of my bare hand close to the ground, like you’re checking a child for fever, because a hand is the best thermometer ever made and it’s free. You can’t see fire in the roots. Brush has roots like a nervous system, down and down, woven through the dirt, and a fire can crawl into them and lie there, eating very slowly, a coal the size of your thumb in a tunnel the width of a pencil. For days. Sometimes, in the old stories, for weeks.
It is the most boring work in the world, mop-up. It is also the only part of the job that ever actually finishes anything.
The department knows this. It’s in the manuals. It’s in the training. Walk the black until it’s cold. Then walk it again.
What the manuals don’t have a chapter for is money.

That December, the week before Christmas, I stood in the maintenance yard downtown with a friend of mine who works there, a mechanic, and we looked at the engines. Rows of them. Fire engines lined up like cattle in a feedlot, some with their hoods open, some with their tyres off, some stripped of their tools, some just waiting for a part that was on order, or would be on order when somebody approved the order. My mechanic friend told me they didn’t have enough people to fix them. He told me there’d been money for mechanics once and then there hadn’t. He said this the way you’d describe the weather.
“How many?” I asked.
He shrugged. “Enough that if the whole city caught fire on the same afternoon, you’d notice.”

We laughed. That’s what you do. Firefighters have the darkest sense of humour of anyone alive except maybe emergency-room nurses and people who work in funeral homes. It’s not cruelty. It’s a pressure valve. If we didn’t laugh we’d have to feel it, and if we felt it we couldn’t go back in.

There is a phrase you’ll hear on the radio at the end of a fire. The incident commander, the person in charge, gets on and says a fire is contained, which means we’ve got a line around it and it shouldn’t get out. Later he says it’s controlled, which means it won’t. Later still somebody says it’s out. Declared out. Those two words close the file. They close the paperwork, they close the overtime, they send the engines home and the crews to bed. They’re the most expensive two words in the job, because every time you say them you’re betting your whole reputation that nothing is breathing under the dirt.
I used to think the words were a promise.
They’re not. They’re a guess with a uniform on.

That December the hills around the station were as dry as I’d seen them in twenty-seven years. You could hear it when you walked through the brush, a sound like somebody crumpling cellophane. We had the conversations you have. The weather service had been putting out warnings all month about wind. The old-timers at the station said the same thing they always say, which is it’s not if, it’s when, and then somebody said when is a long time and somebody else said not that long and then we ate the chili.
On the way out of the yard that day, my mechanic friend tapped the side of an engine with no front wheels.
“Merry Christmas,” he said. “This one’s yours if you want it.”
3. The Letter Omid

The letter from the insurance company came in the same month we buried my father. I remember because I found it on the hall table under the sympathy cards, and for a second I thought it was another sympathy card, and in a way it was.

My parents had been with the same insurance company for forty-four years. My father had paid them every year, on time, by cheque, and then by computer when I set that up for him and he complained about it for a decade. He had never made a claim. Not once. The house had never so much as had a leak. My father used to say that paying insurance was like paying rent to God: you did it so you would never have to meet the landlord.

The letter said, in the soft, round language these letters always use, that after careful review, the company would not be renewing our policy when it expired in the summer. It thanked us for our many years as a valued customer. It suggested we contact an agent to explore our options. It did not say why.
It didn’t need to. By then everybody on the hill had one.

The neighbours talked about it the way you talk about a cold going around the office. The family across the street had one. The dentist two houses down had one. The retired film producer at the top of the road, who had once shown my father his Oscar and let him hold it, had one, and told everyone at the mailboxes that it was an outrage and he would be writing to somebody. The letters had come to hundreds of houses in the Palisades that spring, and thousands more across the state, all from the big companies, one after another, like birds leaving a tree. It didn’t feel like a plan. It felt like weather. That’s the thing about something happening to everybody at once. It stops looking like anyone did it.
Here, in plain words, is what happens when your insurance company leaves you in California.

You call around. The other big companies are not writing new policies in your area, which is an insurance phrase meaning no. Some are not writing new policies anywhere in the state. You are then introduced to something called the FAIR Plan. The name is a little joke the universe plays on you. The FAIR Plan is the state’s insurer of last resort: a pool that all the big private companies are required to pay into, so that people nobody else will insure can still get something. It is the lifeboat. And it is a lifeboat in the way a door floating in the ocean is a lifeboat.

The FAIR Plan covers fire. Mostly fire. It does not cover a lot of other things that your old policy covered, like water damage or theft or somebody slipping on your steps, so you’re supposed to buy a second policy from someone else to fill in the holes, if you can find someone. It costs a great deal more than your old policy. And it has a ceiling. There’s a limit to how much it will pay to rebuild your house, a hard number, no matter what your house is actually worth.
Our house, the steel-and-glass house on the hill, the house built to stand a hundred years, was worth a good deal more than that number.
“How much more?” my wife asked, at the kitchen table, the night I explained it.
I told her.
She was quiet for a while. Then she said, “So if it burns, we lose the difference.”
“If it burns,” I said, “we lose the difference.”
“Will it burn?”
“It’s steel,” I said. “It’s concrete. It’s glass. My father built it.”
Tara was at the table too, doing homework she was not doing. “Glass breaks,” she said, not looking up. “When it gets hot. We did it in chemistry.”
“Physics,” my wife said.
“Whatever. It breaks. Then the fire comes in the hole.”

My mother was at the sink. She didn’t turn around. She said something in Persian, quietly, to the window, and I asked her what it was, and she said it was nothing, it was an old saying, and I didn’t press. I found out months later what she’d said. It was a saying of her grandmother’s from Kashan [kaa-SHAAN], the old desert town in the middle of Iran where her family came from: The one who builds a house of glass should not keep a stove.

We signed up for the FAIR Plan. We bought the second policy to fill in the holes. The two together cost almost three times what my father had paid the year before. We paid it, because we could, which put us ahead of a great many people I would meet in hotel lobbies the next winter. Then we did what everybody does after they’ve paid for protection, which is stop thinking about it.
I’ll tell you one more thing about that summer, because at the time it was nothing.

In July, a man came to the door. Well-dressed, pleasant, fifties, a good watch. He said he represented some buyers who were interested in properties in the Highlands, and he’d heard about my father, and he was sorry for our loss. He said that if we ever thought about selling, he could make it very easy. Cash. No inspections. Quick. He left a card with just a name and a phone number on it, no company, and a line of small grey print underneath that I never read.
I told him we weren’t selling. He said of course, of course, and smiled, and said the thing I didn’t think about again for six months.
“Things change,” he said. “That’s all. Things change up here.”
I put the card in the kitchen drawer with the takeout menus and the dead batteries.
4. New Year’s Eve Ray
On New Year’s Eve the city of Los Angeles bans fireworks, and then the city of Los Angeles sets off approximately all of them.

I was on shift. I’d volunteered, because I’m divorced and my kids are grown and there’s nothing sadder than a man my age watching the ball drop alone in an apartment in Sherman Oaks, and because the young guys with families should be home with them. That’s the other thing about the job nobody puts on the poster. The station is a family, and like most families it runs on who’s willing to take the bad shift.
Around eleven-thirty I went out behind the station to look at the hills. You do that on a night like that. You go out and you smell the air.

The sky over the city was going pop-pop-pop, red and green and gold, from the flats all the way to the ocean. Somebody in the canyon had something with real gunpowder in it, and every few minutes it went off with a thump I could feel in my chest. Every one of those is a small fire in the sky, and every one comes down somewhere. I have pulled a lot of dead palm trees off a lot of roofs on the first of January.

The air was dry. No wind yet, not really. Cold, for us. Clear. And there was a smell coming down off the ridge, faint, that I didn’t recognise at first. Sweet. Heavy. Like flowers left too long in a vase, or a funeral in a greenhouse. I stood there trying to place it. It’s a thing you train yourself to notice, smells. Eucalyptus smells like cough drops. Sage smells like a Thanksgiving turkey. Burning plastic smells like the end of the world. This was none of those.

I walked out to the edge of the lot, where the station backs onto the slope, and looked up. There’s a patch of big wild bushes that grow there, and up the whole trail, big soft grey-green leaves and flowers the size of a coffee mug, white trumpets that open at night. Sacred datura [duh-TOO-ruh]. Jimsonweed, the old cowboys called it. Every part of it is poison. I’ve taken hikers to the emergency room who ate the seeds to see what would happen, and what happened was they saw things, and then they tried to fight a parked car. The flowers open after dark and close in the morning. Moths come to them. They smell like that. Sweet.
The flowers were open. All of them. All the way up the slope, pale in the dark, dozens of them, like a crowd of little white faces turned toward the station.

I remember standing there thinking, that’s not right. Datura flowers in summer. It blooms in the heat, in July, August. I have never seen one open in January. I have never seen one open in December. I stood there for a long time, long enough that one of the younger guys, a probationer, which is what we call a firefighter in his first year, still on trial, stuck his head out the back door and asked if I was all right.
“You smell that?” I said.
He sniffed. “Somebody’s weed?”
“No.”
“Then no, Cap.”

I went back inside. The guys were watching the countdown on the TV in the kitchen, the replay from New York, where it had happened three hours before, a big ball of lights dropping over a crowd of people in plastic hats. Somebody had made a cake. I had a piece. It was a bad cake, and I had a second piece, because it was New Year’s Eve and there was nobody to tell me not to.

At midnight everybody in the kitchen said happy new year and shook hands like men do, one hand on your hand and the other on your shoulder, and the fireworks outside went crazy for about ten minutes and then started to thin out.
I was rinsing my plate at the sink when the tones dropped.

The tones are the sound the dispatch system makes before it sends you somewhere. Every firefighter in the world knows that sound in his spine. Your body is moving before your brain has finished hearing it.
The clock on the microwave said 12:12.
Brush fire, the voice said. Reported by callers. Near the top of the trail above the Highlands.

On the way to the engine I looked up through the open bay door, and there it was. A little orange glow, high on the ridge, right where the trail runs along the top toward the rock the hikers call Skull Rock, because it has two holes in it like a face. The glow was small. Pretty, almost. Like a campfire somebody had left.
I have been doing this job for twenty-seven years. I know better than to think anything on a ridge is small.
5. The Flowers on the Ridge Omid

We had an understanding in our family about New Year’s Eve. My wife and Tara went to parties. My mother and I stayed home. We had done it that way for three years, since my wife’s family started having the kind of New Year’s parties that required a coat check, and it suited everybody. My mother didn’t like crowds. I didn’t like my wife’s family. Nobody said so.

So at eleven-thirty on the last night of the year it was just the two of us on the back deck, my mother in her good coat with a blanket over her knees, me with a bottle of wine that cost more than my first car, which is not a boast about the wine. My first car was very bad.

From the deck you could see the whole show. The fireworks went up everywhere, from the village below us, from the flats of Santa Monica, from the Valley over the hills behind, all the way out to where the lights of the city ran into the ocean. They were illegal. Every one of them. The fire department had posted a warning about it on the internet, which is where warnings go to be admired.
“Your father hated this,” my mother said.
“Fireworks?”
“The noise. He said it sounded like the war.”

I didn’t ask which war. My parents had left before the one I knew about. But they had known people, afterward, and my father had gone quiet for a year in the eighties that nobody explained to me, and some things in our family were not talked about in English.

We sat. The fireworks thumped. My mother hummed something under her breath, a piece she used to play when I was small, a nocturne, which is a piece of music written for the night. She has a way of humming that’s more like thinking out loud.
Then the smell came down the hill.

I noticed it first because I notice sounds and smells for a living, or at least I thought I did. It was sweet. It was thick. It was the smell of an expensive hotel lobby, flowers everywhere, too many flowers, the kind of sweetness that tips over into something like rot if you stand in it long enough. It came down off the ridge on a little breath of cold air and settled on the deck like a blanket.
My mother stopped humming. She lifted her head the way deer lift their heads.
“Tātureh [taa-too-REH],” she said.
“What?”
“Tātureh. The flower. The white one.” She pointed up the hill with her chin. “There.”

I looked. At first I couldn’t see anything, just the dark bulk of the ridge above the rooftops of the Highlands, blacker than the sky. Then my eyes adjusted, and I saw them. Up the slope, all along the edge of the trail, pale shapes in the dark. Dozens. Hundreds. White flowers, big as teacups, open to the night, glowing faintly in the light from the city like they had their own small moons inside them.
“Those are open now?” I said. “In the winter?”
“No,” my mother said. “They don’t open in the winter.”
“Then what—“
“They don’t open in the winter,” she said again, patiently, as if I had failed a very easy question, and pulled the blanket higher on her knees.

We sat and looked at the white flowers on the ridge. The smell got heavier. I remember a thought I had, which I’ve had a long time to think about since: that the flowers didn’t look like flowers. They looked like an audience. Like the faces of people in a dark theatre, before the lights come up, turned toward the stage, waiting for the show.

“In Kashan,” my mother said, “my grandmother told us not to go near it. Thieves used it. They put it in your tea, you went to sleep, you woke up with no rug.” She laughed, a little. “She also said the old saints used it. To see.”
“To see what?”
“What was coming.”
“Did it work?”
My mother shrugged, the Persian shrug, which uses the whole face. “The thieves got the rugs.”

At midnight all the fireworks in the world went up at once, and my mother held my hand, and said sāl-e no mobārak [SAAL-eh no mo-baa-RAK], which is happy new year, and I said it back. Her hand was very small and very cold. She’s eighty-four. She said, looking up at the ridge and not at me, “We’ve done this before.”
“We do this every year, Maman [maa-MAAN].” It’s what I have called her since before I could say anything else.
“Yes,” she said. “Every year.”

The fireworks thinned out. The sky went back to being mostly sky. I looked at my phone to see if my wife had texted, and she had, a photo of Tara in a paper crown, and the time on my screen said 12:12.
When I looked up from the phone, the ridge was on fire.
Not much. A small bright orange mark, high up, near the top of the trail, right in the middle of all those pale open flowers. Like somebody had struck a match in the back row of the theatre.
My mother didn’t look surprised. She looked, if anything, like someone who has come into a cinema a little late and found that the film has already started.
“There it is,” she said.
Heard on the Ridge
I am not your enemy. I was your gardener.

Before you came, before the ones who came before you came, I walked these hills every few decades like a man walking the rows of his orchard. I took the old growth, the dead wood, the brush that had died standing up and forgotten to lie down. I left the ground black and clean and warm. And the seeds were waiting for me. You should know this. There are seeds in these hills that will not wake for rain. They will not wake for sun. They sleep in the dirt for fifty years, for a hundred, and they wake for me. For my heat, and for my smoke. There is a poppy here that only blooms after I have passed. There is a small pale-yellow flower the people here call whispering bells, because its dry petals rattle in the wind like somebody saying something very quietly, and it only grows in my footprints. For ten thousand years these hills have been setting a table for me, and I have been coming to supper.

The people who were here first understood this. The Tongva [TONG-vuh] down by the rivers, the Chumash [CHOO-mash] up the coast. They did not love me and they did not fear me. They used me. They let me out in small patches, in the cool months, in the wet months, the way you let a dog out into a yard. A little here. A little there. Enough to open the land for their acorns and their deer, never enough to take a village. It was a conversation. It went on for a very long time.
Then you arrived, and you decided I was a crime.

You were very sincere about it. I will give you that. You saw what I did to a wooden town and you said never again, and you meant it with your whole heart. For a hundred years you arrested me every time I showed my face. You built roads to reach me and airplanes to drown me. You made a bear in a hat and put him on posters and taught your children that only they could stop me. You were proud. Every year you counted how quickly you had caught me, and every year the number was better.
And the brush waited.

It grew, and grew old, and died, and did not lie down, because I was not allowed to come and lay it down. It stood there dead among the living, year after year, piling up. You would call it fuel. I would call it a debt. Every small visit you refused me went into a ledger somewhere in these hills, and the ledger kept perfect accounts, and the ledger did not care who was in office.

I want you to understand something, before any of this begins. I did not choose the size I came back at. You chose it. You simply chose it very slowly, one small victory at a time, and none of you was in charge long enough to see the bill arrive.

I will be fair to you. It is not only the old brush. My hills need me to visit, yes, but not too often, and never like this. You have been letting me in too often in some places now, with your cigarettes and your power lines and your fireworks, and a hill I visit every few years does not grow back as brush at all. It grows back as weeds, and weeds are only a faster fuse. So do not imagine the answer is simply more of me. The answer was always the right amount of me, in the right season, with somebody watching. You had that once. It was called a conversation. You stopped having it.
And you built on the table while it was still set.

I have watched you for a long time. I notice things. It is the only thing I can do between visits. I notice that you build your houses where my winds come down the canyons like water down a drain. I notice you build them of wood, and roof them with things that catch. I notice that you plant beautiful trees against your windows, and the trees are full of oil.
I noticed, this last spring, the postman.

He came up the long road into the high neighbourhood more often than usual. He put a great many envelopes into a great many mailboxes, all the same shape, all the same colour, all from a small number of very large companies. I don’t read. But I know the smell of fear in a house, and it changed in a great many houses that spring, on the same few days, as if a wind had come through.
I also noticed, in the summer, a man with a good watch walking door to door.
I am only telling you what I noticed. I am a witness. I am not a judge. What men intend is not a thing I can see. I can only see what they leave for me.

The hills are ready. They have been ready for a long time. The table is set, and the flowers on the ridge have opened out of season to watch, and somewhere below me, in a glass house on a steel frame, a woman whose name is my name is holding her son’s hand in the cold.
I did not choose the night. I want that written down, if anyone is writing.
Somebody else struck the match.
II. DECLARED OUT
6. Hot to the Touch Ray
A fire on a ridge at night is the most beautiful thing you will ever be paid to hate.

We came up the trail road in the dark with the engine grinding in low gear, and the fire sat above us on the crest like a necklace somebody had dropped, a thin bright line of orange beads strung along the top of the hill, glowing and going dim and glowing again as the little breeze breathed on it. Below it, the whole of the city spread out to the ocean in lights. Above it, stars. You could sell that picture. People do.

It was a small fire. Eight acres, maybe. An acre is about the size of a football field without the end zones, so picture eight of those, laid across a steep hillside of brush and grass in the dark, burning slowly, the way a cigarette burns when nobody’s smoking it. No wind to speak of, thank God. On a windy night that same fire would have been in the Highlands in twenty minutes, and I’d be telling you a different story.

We did it the way you do it. We ran hose up the trail, hundreds of feet of it, men hauling it over their shoulders like fat canvas snakes, and we fought the edge of the fire where it tried to creep downhill toward the houses. A helicopter came in, which surprised some of the young guys, because they think helicopters don’t fly at night. Ours do, when it’s calm. It came in low with its big light on, like a lighthouse that had decided to go for a walk, and dropped water on the hottest part of the line, and the water came down through the searchlight silver and slow and hissed where it landed, and a cloud of white steam went up and blew away over the ridge. The probationer next to me said holy shit, softly, reverently, like he was in church. That’s the right response. I’ve seen a thousand water drops and I still say it, inside.
By four in the morning we had a line around it. By sunrise it was contained. The incident commander got on the radio and said so, and everybody on the hill breathed out at once.
Then came mop-up.
I want to tell you about January second exactly, because I have been over it so many times since that it has worn smooth, like a coin you keep in your pocket and turn over with your thumb.

We walked the black. That’s what you do. Hand tools, a hose still charged, a line of us across the burn going slowly uphill in the cold morning. The ground was grey and black and powdery, like the inside of a fireplace, and the stumps of the burned brush stuck up out of it like the bristles of a burnt broom. And it was warm. You notice that. The ground in a burn the next day is warm the way a bed is warm after somebody has just got out of it.

The probationer found it first. He was working a patch of bigger stumps near the top, old chaparral with thick woody bases, some of it half a century old, and he took off his glove the way I’d taught him and held his hand over the ground, and then he looked up at me with a strange expression.
“Cap,” he said. “It’s hot.”

I went over. I took off my glove. He was right. Not warm. Hot. A little wisp of something that was either smoke or steam came out of a crack in the dirt beside a stump and curled away in the air. I put my hand on a rock, a grey rock about the size of a loaf of bread, and pulled it back. The rock was hot to the touch. The sun had been up for three hours and it was January and that rock had no business being that hot.
“Roots,” I said.
He nodded. He’d been listening in training. “Burning in the roots.”
“Maybe. Maybe it’s just holding heat. Rocks do that.” I didn’t believe it as I said it. I’ve said a lot of things I didn’t believe on a hillside. It’s another of the pressure valves.

We started digging. That’s the answer to a hot stump: you dig it out, you open the ground, you spread the coals, you drown them. It’s slow and it’s filthy and it’s the only way. We’d been at it about twenty minutes when the chief came up the trail.

I’m not going to give you his name. He’s not a bad man. I’ve known him fifteen years. He came up the trail in a clean jacket with a radio on his hip and a look on his face I recognised, which is the look of a man who has been on the phone since six o’clock with people who do not walk hillsides.
He told us to pack it up. Roll the hose. Pick up the equipment. We were done here.
I told him about the hot ground. I told him about the rock.

He listened. I’ll give him that too. He listened, and then he said a thing about this being parkland, and there being plants up here that were protected, rare ones, and the people who look after the park being unhappy about us tearing up the hillside with hand tools and flooding it with water. He said the fire was out. He said crews had been over it all night. He said it was contained and controlled and there was nothing more to do here that was worth the damage we’d do doing it.
I want you to hold on to that for a second, because I have been holding on to it for a long time. We were told to stop digging so we wouldn’t hurt the plants.
“Chief,” I said. “This is a bad idea.”

I said those words. I know I said them because I’ve heard them in my head every day since, in my own voice, which sounds more reasonable in my head than it did on the hill. This is a bad idea. Five words. They were exactly the right five words and they did exactly nothing.

He looked at the ground. He looked at me. He said the same thing again, in the same tone, which is how orders get said a second time. And I did what twenty-seven years of this job had trained into me deeper than any manual, which is that when a chief tells you twice, you do it. There’s a reason for that. On a fire you can’t have a crew arguing. People die when a crew argues. The whole thing runs on doing what you’re told when you’re told it, and trusting the man above you to have seen something you haven’t.
So we rolled the hose.

It took about two hours. We picked up every piece of equipment on that hill. The probationer didn’t say anything. He didn’t have to. He rolled his line very slowly and very neatly, which is what young firefighters do instead of arguing, and every few minutes he looked up at the patch of stumps where the ground was hot.
When we pulled out, the clock on the dashboard said 12:12. Noon.
On the radio later that afternoon, the fire was declared out.
Declared out. I told you about those words. They close the file. They close the paperwork. They send everybody home to bed.

The next day somebody called in smoke up there, a hiker, and a crew went up and looked around and didn’t find anything and came back down. I heard about it at the station, over coffee, and somebody said hikers, the way you’d say tourists, and everybody nodded. I nodded. I’d like to tell you I didn’t. I nodded.

That’s what it looks like, if you were wondering. The end of the world. It looks like a man in a clean jacket who doesn’t want to damage some plants, and five men rolling hose very neatly, and a clock on a dashboard, and a captain nodding over coffee.
It doesn’t look like anything at all.
7. Particularly Dangerous Omid
For five days after New Year’s there was a black patch on the ridge above our house, like a bruise on a green arm.

You could see it from everywhere. From the deck, from the kitchen, from Tara’s bedroom window, from the bottom of Palisades Drive if you knew where to look. A dark smudge up near the top of the trail, surrounded by gold grass and grey-green brush and, still, impossibly, those white flowers, which went on opening every night as if the fire had been a rumour. People on the street talked about it at the mailboxes for about a day. Then they stopped talking about it, because the fire was out. The news said so. The fire department had said so. It had been small, and it was out, and it was a new year.
On the fourth, a Saturday, Tara and I hiked up to look.

This was her idea. She’d become interested in the black patch in the way sixteen-year-olds become interested in things their parents are nervous about. She wanted to see what a fire left behind. I said it was probably closed. She said it wasn’t. She was right; nothing was closed, there was no tape, no sign, nobody. We went up the trail in the late morning, the same trail I’d hiked a thousand times as a boy with my father, him in his terrible white sneakers explaining the engineering of retaining walls to me whether I wanted it or not.

The burn scar was bigger up close than it looked from the house. The ground was grey powder. The brush was burned down to black stumps. It smelled like an old barbecue, and underneath that, faintly, sweet. Tara walked into it in her good shoes, which I pointed out, and she ignored me, which she pointed out.
“It’s so quiet,” she said.
It was. No birds. Nothing moving. Just the sound of the wind, very light, going over the top of the ridge.
Then she said, “Dad. Look.”

She was pointing at the ground near a big burned stump. A thin grey thread of smoke was rising out of the dirt. Not much. A ribbon. You’d miss it if you weren’t standing right over it. It came up out of a crack beside the stump and went straight up for a foot or so and then the breeze took it and it was gone.
“Is that still burning?” she said.
“No,” I said. “It’s out. They said it’s out.”
“Then what’s that?”

I didn’t know what that was. I’m a sound engineer. I stood there and listened to it, which was stupid, because smoke doesn’t make a sound. I thought about calling someone. I actually took my phone out. And then I thought about how I would sound, calling the fire department to say that I had found a small thread of smoke in the exact place where the fire department had just finished putting out a fire, and that I, a man who makes explosions for movie trailers, felt they should come back and do it properly.
I put the phone away.
“It’s probably steam,” I said. “From the ground. It’s cold up here and the ground’s still warm.”
Tara looked at me the way my mother looks at me. It skipped a generation and landed on her whole.
“Steam,” she said.
“Probably.”

We went back down. I thought about the smoke for about an hour, and then I thought about lunch, and then I didn’t think about it again until a hotel room in Santa Monica, three days later, when I thought about nothing else.
The warnings got loud on the Sunday.

Here is a thing I learned that week: the weather service has a ladder of words for how bad things are going to get, and the words at the top of the ladder are almost never used. There’s a fire weather watch, which means be aware. There’s a red flag warning, which means conditions are extremely dangerous for fire. And then, above that, rarely, only a handful of times in a decade, there’s a phrase that sounds like something a bureaucrat would say about a parking garage: a particularly dangerous situation.
On Monday the sixth, the weather service used it.

They said the Santa Ana [SAN-tuh AN-uh] winds were coming. They said the winds would arrive that night and blow hardest on Tuesday and into Wednesday. They said the gusts in the mountains could be as strong as a hurricane’s. They said the air would be so dry it would feel like a desert. They said, in the careful way these people talk, that any fire that started would spread extremely rapidly and be very difficult or impossible to control.
I read this on my phone in the kitchen. My mother was standing at the window. She’d been standing at the window a lot.
“Maman,” I said. “They’re saying the wind is coming.”
“I know,” she said.
“How do you know?”

She didn’t answer. She was looking up at the ridge, at the black patch and the white flowers. After a while she went into the study, which had been my father’s study, and I heard drawers opening. When I looked in later she had taken all the photograph albums off the shelves, all forty-five years of them, the ones from Tehran and the ones from here, and stacked them on the desk in a neat tower beside a canvas bag. She hadn’t put them in the bag. She’d just stacked them next to it, like somebody who has packed for a journey and not yet decided to go.
“What are you doing?” I said.
“Nothing,” she said. “Tidying.”

That evening I checked the cameras. We had six. I’d put them in after my father died, in a fit of something I told myself was prudence and was probably grief: one on the front gate, one on the driveway, one on the back deck looking up the hill, one on the side yard, one in the garage, one in the living room looking out through the big glass. They talked to an app on my phone. You could open the app anywhere in the world and see your house, live, six little windows in a grid. CAM 1, CAM 2, CAM 3. My house as a surveillance feed. I used to check it from work sometimes, for no reason, just to see it standing there.
That night, the wind came.

It came around nine. You could hear it arrive, a long soft roar in the canyon like the sound of a big truck on a freeway a long way off, and then the first gust hit the glass at the back of the house and the whole wall hummed. Hummed. Like a tuning fork. My father had designed that glass for earthquakes, not for this. The palms on the street started to thrash. Something metal went skittering down the road. A trash can, probably. Somebody’s patio chair.

At about eleven the power flickered. Off, on, off, on. When it settled, every clock in the kitchen was blinking. The microwave, the oven, the coffee machine, all flashing the same number at me in green and red, the way they do after an outage, when they’ve lost their minds and have to be told again what time it is.
I meant to reset them. I didn’t. It was late, and the wind was loud, and I thought, tomorrow.
8. The Holdover Ray

There’s a thing the department does before a big wind, or it used to do. It’s called pre-deployment, and it’s exactly what it sounds like: you put the engines where the fire is going to be before the fire gets there.

It’s not complicated. You look at the forecast. You look at the map. You know which hills are dry and which canyons funnel the wind, because you’ve been fighting fires in those canyons your whole career. So you take extra engines and you park them there, in the danger areas, with crews on them, ready. You bring in extra people to staff them. And the simplest way to get extra people is this: when a shift ends, you don’t send it home. You hold it over. The men who worked yesterday stay on today, and the men coming in for today come in anyway, and for a day or two you have twice as many firefighters as usual. It costs overtime. It is the cheapest insurance in the world.

We’d done it before. I’d done it before. Years ago, in a bad wind, I remember the whole station yard full of engines from other parts of the city, men I didn’t know sleeping on cots in the day room, everybody drinking bad coffee and waiting for a fire that, that time, never came. Nobody complained. That’s the thing about pre-deployment: when it works, it looks like nothing happened, and people wonder what they paid for.
On the sixth of January, the day the weather service said particularly dangerous situation, I waited for it.

Some extra engines went out. A handful. To other parts of the city, the Valley, the hills over Hollywood, places where somebody had decided the fire would be. None came to the Palisades. None came to us. The extra engines that were supposed to be staffed mostly weren’t, because the shift that could have staffed them went home. They sent the outgoing shift home.

I asked about it. You’re allowed to ask. I called a friend of mine who works closer to the top than I do, and I asked him, carefully, the way you ask these things, whether anybody was going to hold the shift over, and whether anybody was going to send us some iron. Iron is what we call engines.

He said a lot of things, and they added up to no. He said the engines were in the yard. He said the ones in the yard didn’t have wheels, some of them, or tools, or parts. He said there wasn’t the money for the overtime, or there hadn’t been, or there might be but nobody had signed for it. He said they had people. He said they had a plan.
“What’s the plan?” I said.
“Respond,” he said.

I thought that was funny. I still think that was funny. Sometimes a man tells you the whole truth of the world by accident in one word, and all you can do is laugh at it, because the alternative is to drive downtown and start kicking in doors.

The Mayor, I found out later, was out of the country that week. On an official trip, on the other side of an ocean, which had been planned for months, and which had nothing to do with anything, and which I only mention because a great many people were going to mention it very loudly for a very long time. I don’t think the Mayor would have held the shift over. I don’t think mayors know what a shift is. I just want it on the record that on the night the wind came, the person in charge of the city was somewhere with a different time zone, and the person in charge of the department was somewhere with a phone, and the person in charge of the engine at the bottom of the Palisades was me.
I made chili. That’s the other part of the plan.

We watched the weather on the TV in the day room. There was a lady in a red dress in front of a map of Southern California covered in purple swirls, and every time she said wind one of the young guys said drink, and then they stopped doing that because it wasn’t funny anymore. Around nine the first gusts came through and the bay doors started to rattle in their tracks. The flag outside was standing straight out from the pole like it had been ironed that way.

I went to bed around eleven. You try to sleep before a big day. I lay on my back in the dark in the little captain’s room and listened to the wind working at the building, finding every seam, every loose sheet of metal on the roof, every crack under every door. It sounds like breathing, a Santa Ana. Big slow breaths, and then a gust like somebody shoving a shoulder into the wall.
I thought about the ridge.

I thought about the patch of stumps near the top, where the ground had been hot, and the rock the size of a loaf of bread. I thought about roots running down into the dark under that hill like wires in a wall. I thought about a coal the size of my thumb in a tunnel the width of a pencil, lying there for six days, very patient, very small, eating very slowly, the way I’d told the probationer they could, the way the old men had told me.
I thought, it’s out. It was declared out.
I thought, a guess with a uniform on.

I got up at some point. I don’t know when. I went and stood in the open bay in my socks and looked up at the hill. It was dark. There was nothing up there. No glow, no spark, nothing but the black shape of the ridge against the stars, and the wind pouring down off it so hard I had to lean into it to stand straight. The white flowers were still open. I could see them, faint, all the way up the trail, trembling in the wind, turned toward us.
When I went back to bed, the clock by the cot said 12:12.
I remember thinking that was the third time that week. I remember thinking it didn’t mean anything. Clocks say all kinds of things.
9. Ten Thirty Omid
On the morning of January seventh the sky was the colour of a dirty nickel and the wind was trying to take the house off the hill.

I don’t know how else to say it. I’d lived there my whole life and I had never heard the house make the sounds it made that morning. The glass boomed. The steel frame creaked like a ship. Things I didn’t know could move were moving — the heavy outdoor furniture on the deck slid a foot toward the railing on its own and stopped there, trembling. Out on the street, a palm frond as long as a canoe came down out of the sky and lay across a neighbour’s car like a dead thing. The air was full of dust and leaves and bits of other people’s gardens, all of it racing west toward the ocean.

It was dry. I mean the air itself. My lips cracked. My eyes itched. My mother’s hands, when she poured the tea, had gone papery overnight, and she kept rubbing lotion into them and it kept disappearing.

My wife had gone to work in Santa Monica early. Tara had gone to school. The high school is down the hill, near the village, and it didn’t occur to anybody to keep her home, because nobody keeps their kids home for wind. It’s Los Angeles. We have wind the way other places have snow. You complain about it, you drive carefully, you go to work.
The clocks in the kitchen were still blinking 12:12. I noticed them when I made coffee and thought, I should fix those, and didn’t.

I worked from home that morning, or tried to. I had a trailer due — a big dumb action movie, a building coming down in slow motion, three seconds of glass and fire that I’d been layering for a week. I had my headphones on. I had the sound of a skyscraper exploding in my ears, and I was trying to decide whether it needed more low end, more of that chest-thump you feel in a cinema seat, when my mother touched my shoulder.
I took the headphones off. The wind rushed back in, enormous.
She didn’t say anything. She just pointed through the glass, up the hill.
On the ridge, right where the black patch was, right where the white flowers were, a little puff of grey smoke was rising.

Small. It looked like somebody had lit a cigarette up there. A single grey feather standing up off the crest. Then the wind caught it and it lay down flat and streamed sideways toward the east, and for a second I thought it had gone out. Then it stood up again, and it was darker, and wider, and at its root, just for a moment, I saw a flicker of orange, very bright against the grey brush.
I looked at the clock on my laptop. 10:30.
I remember thinking, very clearly, like a sentence on a screen: That’s the same place.
“It came back,” my mother said.
“What?”
“It came back,” she said again, calmly, and she went to the study and I heard her open the canvas bag.

I called 911. I got a recording. I called again. I got a person, a woman who sounded like she had been answering this call for some time already, and I told her there was a fire on the ridge above the Palisades Highlands and she said yes sir, we’re aware, and asked me to stay on the line, and then the line did something and I was talking to nobody.
When I looked up from the phone, the grey feather was gone.
In its place was a wall.

I don’t know how long it took. A minute. Two. I have gone over the footage since, the camera on the back deck, CAM 3, looking straight up the hill, and I know from the timestamps that it took four minutes from the first puff to the thing I saw next, but four minutes is not how long it took. It took no time at all. The smoke stood up off the ridge, and it was brown now, the colour of a bruise, and it was as wide as the ridge itself, and the wind bent the whole thing over like a hand pushing down on the back of a man’s neck, and it lay down across the top of the hill and started coming toward us.

There was a sound. Under the wind. I’m a sound engineer, and I’d been listening for twenty years to fake versions of this sound, and I’d been wrong about all of them. It wasn’t a roar. It was lower than that. It was like a train going through a tunnel somewhere under the house, a deep continuous rumbling that you felt in your teeth more than you heard, and on top of it, faintly, a crackling like an enormous amount of cellophane being slowly crushed.
The white flowers on the ridge went first. I saw them. All those pale faces turned toward the house, and then the brown smoke went over them, and then they weren’t there.
“Maman,” I said. “Get your coat.”

“I have it,” she said, behind me. She was already wearing it. The canvas bag was over her shoulder, and it was heavy, and I knew without asking that the photograph albums were in it now, all of them, forty-five years, the ones from Tehran and the ones from here.
“How did you know?” I said.

My mother looked at me with an expression I’ve been trying to describe ever since, and the best I can do is this. It was the face of someone watching a film they’ve seen before, at the part they’ve been dreading, and wishing, the way everybody wishes at that part, that this time it will go differently.
“Get the car,” she said. “Get Tara.”

On my phone, the camera app was still open. Six little windows in a grid. CAM 3 showed the back deck, the outdoor furniture shivering against the rail, and above it the whole hillside, and above that a sky that had turned from nickel to brown to a deep, grainy, impossible orange, like a photograph left out in the sun for fifty years.
In the bottom corner of every window, in small white numbers, the cameras were keeping time.
Heard in the Canyon
Let me tell you about my wind, since you never ask.

In the autumn and the winter, far away to the north and east of you, over the high cold deserts where nobody lives, the air grows heavy. It piles up there like water behind a dam. And when it is heavy enough, it spills. It pours down off the high country toward the sea, the way water pours downhill, and as it falls it is squeezed, and as it is squeezed it grows warm, and as it grows warm it grows thirsty. By the time it reaches your mountains it has been falling for hundreds of miles, and it has no water left in it at all. It is the driest air on earth. It drinks from everything it touches. It drinks from the grass and the brush and the leaves on your trees, and from the skin on the backs of your hands, and from your eyes. Then it finds your canyons, which run down to the ocean like gutters, and it squeezes through them, faster and faster, the way your thumb over the end of a garden hose makes the water fly.
You call it the Santa Ana. You named it after a saint. That tells me everything I need to know about how well you understand it.

It comes when your hills are driest. That is the part you keep forgetting. Your rains come in the winter, when they come at all, and your wind comes in the autumn and the early winter, before the rains, when everything that grew in the spring has had all summer to die. So my wind arrives at the one moment in the year when the table is most completely laid. This is not an accident, and it is not a punishment. It is a calendar. It has been the same calendar for longer than you have had calendars.

I remember a morning in November of 1961. The wind came down the canyons above Bel Air, which is only a few ridges east of where I am speaking to you now, and the air was so dry that I burned in near silence. The people who were there said afterward that I made no crackle. I simply walked. I walked through six thousand acres and four hundred and eighty-four homes, most of them on the first day, and I will tell you what I ate first. I ate the roofs. You had roofed your beautiful houses in thin cedar shingles, because they looked handsome, and they were the driest wood in the city, laid out across the top of every house like kindling in a tray. My embers rode the wind ahead of me, hundreds of yards ahead of me, and landed on the shingles, and the houses caught from the top down, and your firefighters stood in the streets with their hoses and watched me arrive on the roofs of houses I had not yet reached.

A young firefighter was standing on one of those streets. His hands shook afterward, for the rest of his life, a little, when he held a cup. He had a son. The son became a firefighter too. I have met them both.

Afterward, you learned something. I will give you that. You began, slowly, to forbid wooden roofs. You made a law that said people must cut back the brush around their homes. For a while you were very careful. You were always very careful for a while.
Then you built more houses higher in the hills, and the brush grew back behind them, and you forgot.
I want to tell you what I noticed this week, because I have been lying very quietly in the dark for six days, and there is nothing to do in the dark but notice.

I noticed that the men who dug at me on the second morning were told to stop. I heard one of them say it was a bad idea. I heard the other one say it again, the same words, in the same tone. I heard the hoses being rolled. I lay in my small tunnel, no wider than a pencil, under the root of an old bush that has been growing on that ridge since before the man who ordered them away was born, and I listened to their boots going back down the hill.
I noticed that in a yard far across the city, a great many red trucks were sleeping with their wheels off.
I noticed that on the night the wind came, the men who could have waited for me were sent home to their beds.
I noticed that the one who was in charge of the whole city was across an ocean, and that the one in charge of the whole state was a long way off too, talking into microphones about something else.
I am not telling you that anyone wanted me to come. I cannot see into your hearts. I can only see what you leave lying around, and you left a great deal lying around.

And I noticed, one more thing, and I will tell you because it has been troubling me: the white flowers on the ridge were open. They do not open in the winter. I have walked those hills for ten thousand years and I have never once seen them open in the winter. They were open all week. They were turned toward the houses, like people waiting for a show to begin.
I do not know who they were waiting for.
It was not me. I was already there.
III. THE CAMERAS
10. It Started Up Again Ray
The phone rang in the station at ten-thirty and a captain from another station said six words I have never been able to get out of my head.
“The Lachman fire started up again.”

That’s what we’d called it, the New Year’s one. The Lachman fire, after a road near where it began. He said it the way you’d say the dog got out again. I didn’t answer him. I was already looking out of the bay door and up the hill, and there it was, exactly where I had stood in my socks the night before and seen nothing: a grey feather on the ridge, lying down flat in the wind, and at the root of it a flicker of orange so bright it looked like a pilot light.
The tones dropped a second later. By then I was in the engine.

I want to explain something about wind, because people who haven’t been in a Santa Ana think they understand wind, and they don’t. They think of a breeze that gets strong. This is not that. This is a river of air coming down the mountain, and it doesn’t blow so much as shove. It shoved the engine sideways on the road. It picked up the gravel on the shoulder and threw it at the windshield like buckshot. When I opened my door at the bottom of the trail it took the door out of my hand and slammed it against its hinges hard enough to crack the paint.
And it picked up the fire and threw it.

Here is the thing nobody understands until they’ve seen it. A wind-driven fire does not walk down a hill like a line of soldiers. It jumps. The wind tears burning pieces off the front of it — bark, leaves, bits of brush, anything light enough to carry — and throws them ahead, a hundred yards, a quarter mile, sometimes a mile, into dry brush or onto a roof or into a gutter full of dead leaves. Each one of those is a new fire. By the time you’ve driven to where the fire was, it’s already somewhere else, in six places, behind you.
We call them embers. It sounds so small. It sounds like something in a fireplace.

We got the engine up as far as we could on the Highlands side. I looked up the slope toward the black patch from New Year’s and it was gone, covered, the whole top of the ridge under a moving roof of brown smoke, and under that roof the fire was coming down through the brush faster than a man can run. Not walking. Running, the way water runs when a dam goes. The sound was a freight train in a tunnel. The heat reached us before the flames did, a hot hand pressed flat against my face at three hundred yards.
The probationer stood next to me with his mouth open. I didn’t say anything to him. There wasn’t anything to say.

I called for more engines. Everybody was calling for more engines. The radio sounded like an airport on Christmas Eve, every voice talking at once, every voice asking for the same thing, and the answer that came back, when an answer came back, was a version of nothing available. The planes couldn’t fly. The big air tankers, the ones that drop the red powder that slows a fire down, can’t fly in winds like that; they’d be thrown into the hills. The helicopters flew when they could, in the gaps between gusts, and then they didn’t. For hours, on the worst day of my life, I looked up at an empty sky.
Remember the plan. Respond.

We responded. That’s the truth, and I don’t want anybody reading this to think the men on the ground didn’t fight. They fought like animals. They fought with what they had. The problem wasn’t the fighting. The problem was that there were six fires in the Highlands and then twenty and then I stopped counting, and there were not enough of us to be in twenty places, and the ones who could have been were at home in bed, or in the yard downtown with no wheels, or across the city waiting for a fire that somebody had decided would happen somewhere else.

At one point, around noon, I stood on a corner in the Highlands with my crew and I watched a spot fire start in a hedge. That’s one of those new little fires an ember lights when it lands. I looked at my hose, and I looked at the house behind the hedge, and I looked at the next house, and the one after, and I understood a thing that I had known in theory for twenty-seven years and had never had to know in my body.
We were not going to stop this. We were going to choose.
I’ll tell you about the choosing later. I’m not ready yet.

On the dashboard of the engine, the clock was keeping time the way clocks do, not interested. Some time after noon I looked at it for no reason, and it said 12:12, and I remember thinking that the day seemed to have been going on for a hundred years, and it was only lunchtime.
11. Palisades Drive Omid

There is one road out of the Highlands. It’s called Palisades Drive. It curls down the canyon from the top of the neighbourhood to Sunset Boulevard at the bottom, two lanes, sometimes four, lined with eucalyptus and pine and very expensive landscaping, and on a normal day it takes about eight minutes to drive. On January seventh it took most people more than an hour, and some people never finished it.

I put my mother in the car. She sat in the passenger seat with the canvas bag of photograph albums on her knees like a small, heavy child. I backed out of the driveway and stopped at the bottom of it and looked back at the house, because you do. I thought, clearly, I’ll be back tonight. I thought it the way you think the plane will land.

My phone buzzed in my pocket, and buzzed again. Everybody’s phone was buzzing. It was the evacuation order, the official one, telling us to leave now, which we had already done, which everybody on the hill had already done, because there was a wall of brown smoke coming down over the top of the neighbourhood and nobody needed a text message to explain it.

Tara’s school is down the hill, near the village. I called her. She answered on the first ring, which she has never once done in her life. She said they were letting them go, the kids with cars were leaving, she was going to walk down to the Pacific Coast Highway with her friends. I told her not to walk. She said, “Dad, nobody’s driving anywhere,” and then she put the phone to the window of a classroom, and I heard it, the sound of every car horn on the Westside going at once.
“Walk,” I said. “Walk to the ocean. Stay with your friends. Mom will come for you from Santa Monica. Don’t stop to film anything.”
“I’m not an idiot,” she said, and hung up, and I loved her so much it hurt my teeth.
Then I turned onto Palisades Drive and joined the end of the line.

I want you to picture it. Two lanes of cars, then four, nose to tail, all pointed downhill, not moving. Mercedes and Teslas and minivans and a landscaper’s truck with the mowers still on the back. People in bathrobes. People with dogs on their laps and cats in pillowcases and parrots in cages on the passenger seat. A man in a golf cart. An old woman with an oxygen tank. The sky had gone orange-brown, and the light coming through it was the colour of weak tea, and in that light everybody looked yellow and sick, like figures in an old photograph.
And on both sides of the road, the hills were burning.

Not far away. Right there. I could see the flames in the brush on the slope above us, fifty yards off, then forty, moving along the hillside faster than we were moving down the road. Embers blew across the windshield like orange snow. A palm tree at the side of the road caught all at once, from the top down, the dead fronds at its crown going up like a struck match, and the burning fronds came off in the wind and sailed over the line of cars and landed on the other side.
My mother watched it through the window without speaking.

We moved ten feet. We stopped. We moved ten feet. The car ahead of us was a white SUV with a family inside, two little boys in the back seat staring at us out of the rear window, and I made a face at them, the way you would on any road trip, and one of them almost smiled.
After twenty minutes, people started getting out.

It started ahead of us, around a bend. First one door opened, then another. People stepped out of their cars and stood in the road and looked down the hill at the line that wasn’t moving and looked up the hill at the fire that was, and they made a calculation, and they started to walk. Then to run. Carrying children, carrying bags, carrying nothing. They left their cars in the road with the doors open, some of them with the engines still running, and ran down Palisades Drive toward the ocean between the rows of stopped cars.
“Maman,” I said.
“I know,” she said.
“You can’t run.”
“No,” she agreed. “I can walk.”

She’s eighty-four. She had a hip replaced four years ago. She walks to the mailbox and back in the mornings and complains about it. And she opened the car door, into that wind, and got out, and stood in the road with the canvas bag over her shoulder and her good coat buttoned up to her chin, and looked at me through the window as if to ask what I was waiting for.

A firefighter came up the line between the cars, walking fast, shouting. He was telling people to leave the keys in the ignition. Leave your keys, leave your keys. I didn’t understand at first. Later I learned that the abandoned cars had jammed the road so completely that the fire engines coming up couldn’t get through, and they were going to bring in a bulldozer to push the cars aside like toys, and a car without its keys is a car that can’t be moved. I heard afterwards that the bulldozer came, and did exactly that, and I have seen the pictures: expensive cars shoved into a heap at the side of the road like a child’s collection swept off a table.
I left the keys in the ignition. I got out. I took my mother’s arm.

We walked down Palisades Drive together through the smoke, an old Persian woman in a good coat and her middle-aged son, among the stopped cars and the running people and the burning hills, and every fifty yards or so she stopped to catch her breath, and while she caught it she looked around at everything with the same calm, watchful expression, as if she were memorising it for a test.

About halfway down, a pickup truck pulled out of a driveway and stopped beside us. A young man, a stranger, Latino, maybe twenty-five, a landscaper by the look of his truck. He said, “Get in, get in,” and we got in, my mother in the cab and me in the back among the rakes, and he drove us down the wrong side of the road, the uphill side, which was empty, with his hazard lights going, all the way to Sunset.
I never got his name. I’ve thought about him every day since.
At the bottom, on the Pacific Coast Highway, with the ocean on one side and the fire on the other, I found a text from my wife. She had Tara. They were in Santa Monica. They were fine.
I looked at the time. It was 12:12.
12. Soft Hydrants Ray
I promised I’d tell you about the choosing.

By the middle of the afternoon the fire was in the neighbourhoods, and the thing you need to understand about a fire in a neighbourhood is that after a certain point it stops being a wildfire at all. The brush has burned. What’s burning now is houses, and houses set other houses on fire. A burning house throws off embers like a bonfire and heat like a furnace, and if the next house is close enough, and it usually is, the next house catches too. Then that one catches the next. We call it house-to-house. Once it gets going it doesn’t need the hills anymore. It feeds itself, street by street, like a line of dominoes that knocks itself down.
So you choose.

You stand at the end of a street with one engine and four men and one hose, and you look at the houses, and you decide which ones you can save and which ones you can’t. You look for the ones with a gap around them, a lawn, a driveway, no trees against the walls. You look for a tile roof instead of wood. You look at which way the wind is going. And you pick. You put your water on the house you think you can hold, and you let the house next to it go, and you don’t look at the house you let go, because if you look at it you’ll see somebody’s Christmas lights still up in the window and somebody’s bicycle in the driveway, and you’ll stop being useful.

There’s a word for this in the manuals. Triage. It’s a medical word. It’s what they do on battlefields, when there are more wounded than doctors, and somebody has to decide who gets saved first. I always thought it was a strange word to find in a fire manual. I don’t anymore.
And then the water went soft.

That’s what we call it. You open the hydrant and hook up and you get a good strong stream, and then, a few minutes later, it starts to weaken. The hose goes limp in your hands like a snake that’s died. The stream falls short of the roof, then short of the wall, then just dribbles out of the nozzle onto your boots. You check the hydrant. It’s open. There’s just nothing coming.

Here’s why, in plain words, because the arguments about it went on for a year afterward and most of them were shouting. The water for the high part of the Palisades comes up the hill in pipes and gets stored in big tanks at the top, so that gravity can push it back down to the houses and the hydrants. The system was built to fill bathtubs and water lawns and put out a house fire or two. It was never built for hundreds of houses burning at once, with every hydrant in the neighbourhood wide open, and burned-out homes pouring water out of melted pipes into the dirt. The tanks drained faster than the pumps could fill them. When the tanks ran dry, the hydrants uphill ran dry. Simple as that.

And above the neighbourhood, up a canyon, there was a reservoir. A big one. The size of a lake. It had been sitting empty for most of a year, because its cover had a tear in it and the city was waiting to fix it. I didn’t know that on the day. I found it out later, like everybody, on the news.
