Later still, some very serious people wrote a very serious report saying that even if the reservoir had been full it wouldn’t have been enough — it would have helped for a while, they said, and then the hydrants would have gone soft anyway, because nothing built to fill bathtubs could keep up with a burning town.

I believe the report. I’ve read it twice. I also know what it’s like to stand in a driveway with a dead hose in your hands, and I’ll tell you that a man in that position does not want to hear about percentages.

Around three o’clock I was on a steep street near the top of the Highlands, a street of big houses on big lots with big views, and the hydrant in front of one of them went soft on us. It was a strange house. Steel and glass. The whole back wall was windows looking down the canyon to the ocean. Someone had built it to last. You could see that. There were security cameras on it, little white ones, under the eaves and over the gate, and I remember standing in that driveway with the hose going limp in my hands and looking straight up into one of those cameras.

I don’t know why I looked. It was just there, a little glass eye, watching me fail. I thought, somebody’s going to see this. I thought, I’m sorry. I actually thought those words, to a camera, like a man apologising to a stranger he’s bumped on the street.
Then the water stopped, and the pine trees at the side of the house went up like torches, and we got back on the engine and went looking for a hydrant that still had something in it.
The probationer asked me, on the way down, whether the house would make it.
I told him the truth, which is that I didn’t know, and that he should stop asking questions like that, because there’d be a lot more houses before tonight, and he couldn’t carry all of them.
He’s a smart kid. He heard what I meant. He stopped asking, and I could see him carrying all of them anyway.
13. The Cameras Omid

The hotel was in Santa Monica, four blocks from the beach, and they gave us the last room they had at twice the price on their website, and I paid it without arguing, which is the one thing I did right all day.

It was a small room with two beds and a window that looked out on the back of another hotel. My wife and Tara sat on one bed. My mother sat in the only chair with the canvas bag on her knees. I sat on the other bed with my phone. Through the window, over the rooftops to the north, the whole sky was the colour of an infected cut, and ash was falling on the parked cars in the street like grey snow.
I opened the camera app.
Six windows. Six little squares. My house.
I want to describe this as exactly as I can, because it’s the only part of the whole thing I actually saw with my own eyes. Everything else I was somewhere else for.

CAM 1, the front gate, was fine at first. The gate, the plants, the street beyond, all in that strange brown light. Then embers started crossing it. Hundreds of them, left to right, blown sideways by the wind like orange hail, bouncing off the gate and the paving stones, gathering in the corners where the leaves gather. The camera had a microphone. I turned it up. It was the sound I’d heard on the deck that morning, the freight train in the tunnel, and over it the rattle of the embers hitting the metal gate like somebody throwing gravel.

CAM 2, the driveway, showed a fire engine. That was the first thing that made my heart jump. A real fire engine, parked in my driveway, and four men in yellow hooking a hose to the hydrant at the curb. I sat up straight on the hotel bed. I said, “They’re there, they’re at the house,” and my wife came over and Tara came over and we watched them together, four small yellow figures in a small square on a small screen, fighting for our house.

Then the stream from their hose got weak. I watched it happen. I watched it fall short of the roof. I watched one of them, the one in charge I think, older, walk back to the hydrant and check it and stand there. And then — I have watched this recording more times than I can count — he looked up. Straight up, into the camera. His face was black with soot and he was squinting against the smoke and he looked directly at me, through the lens, through the phone, into a hotel room in Santa Monica, for about three seconds.
Then he turned away, and they rolled up the hose, and the engine drove out of the frame.
“Why are they leaving?” Tara said.
Nobody answered her.

CAM 4, the side yard, went next. There were two big pine trees on that side of the house, old ones, my father had planted them when I was a baby, and I watched them catch. They didn’t burn the way wood burns in a fireplace. They exploded. The oil in the needles, I learned later, which is why you’re not supposed to plant pines against a house. They went up with a sound the microphone couldn’t hold — it clipped, it went to a flat roar of static — and the whole square turned white, and then orange, and then black.

CAM 5, the garage, just stopped. No fire, no smoke. The picture froze on an image of my father’s workbench and a box of Christmas decorations, and a little spinning wheel appeared in the middle of the square, and then the words camera offline.

CAM 3, the back deck, was the one I couldn’t stop looking at. It pointed up the hill, the way it always had, at the ridge where the white flowers had been, and there was nothing up there now but a black slope and a moving river of smoke. The furniture on the deck was burning. The railing was burning. And through all of it the camera kept looking up the hill, calm, as if it were still waiting for something to come down.
At 6:40, by the little white numbers in the corner, the big glass wall at the back of the house broke.

I didn’t see it break. CAM 6 was inside, in the living room, looking out through the glass, and I saw the living room fill with orange light, and then I saw the glass go. It didn’t shatter the way glass shatters in the movies. I know. I make those sounds. I’ve layered thirty tracks of shattering glass for a three-second shot. It wasn’t like that. It sagged. It bent inward in the middle like a sheet of plastic in an oven, and a crack ran across it, and then the whole wall simply wasn’t there anymore, and the fire walked in through the hole.
Tara said, very quietly, “Glass breaks. When it gets hot.”

My mother’s piano was in that room. The Steinway. Forty years of other people’s children being told that they were rushing. I watched it on CAM 6. I watched the fire go across the floor toward it, and I watched the lid of the piano catch, and then the picture went brown and then black and then the little wheel came, and the words.
Camera offline.
That left CAM 3. The deck. Looking up the hill.

We sat and watched it for another hour. None of us spoke. My mother never once looked at the phone. She sat in the chair with the photograph albums and looked at the wall, and every so often her lips moved, and I don’t know if she was praying, or doing arithmetic, or talking to my father.

At 7:52, the picture on CAM 3 shook, very slightly, as if something heavy had fallen somewhere in the house. Then the image tilted sideways, slowly, about thirty degrees, and stopped, so that the black hill and the orange sky sat crooked in the square, like a picture hanging badly on a wall.
The numbers in the corner kept counting for another eleven seconds. Then they stopped too.
The last thing my house ever showed me was a crooked view of the hill that burned it.
14. Across the City Ray
At about six that evening a second fire started on the other side of Los Angeles, in the foothills above Altadena, twenty-five miles east of us.

I heard it on the radio the way you’d hear that a second ship had hit an iceberg. There was a pause on the channel, a real pause, the first quiet in eight hours, and then everybody started talking at once again. The Altadena fire was running in the same wind, the same way, down the same kind of hills into the same kind of neighbourhoods. And every engine they might have sent to us, they now had to split in two. That same night a third fire broke out in the Valley, and the next day a fourth in the hills above Hollywood. For a couple of days the whole city looked, from a helicopter, like a birthday cake that somebody had lit at both ends.

I’ve been asked since whether it was the worst thing I ever saw. It wasn’t one thing. That’s what people don’t understand. It was a thousand small things, one after another, for forty hours, and none of them stopped to let you take in the last one.
A swimming pool with a family’s patio furniture floating in it, and the water steaming.
A street where every single house was gone except one, perfectly untouched, its lawn sprinkler still going round and round.

An old man on a roof with a garden hose, refusing to come down, spraying his gutters with a stream of water that wouldn’t have put out a barbecue, while the house next door burned so hot the paint on his side was bubbling. We got him down. I don’t know if he thanked us. I don’t know if he should have.
A dog walking down the middle of Sunset Boulevard, alone, very calmly, in the direction of the ocean, as if it had an appointment.

Some people didn’t get out. I’m not going to write about them. That belongs to their families and not to me. I’ll only say that the number was small compared to the size of the thing, and that every one of them was the whole world to somebody, and that for every one of them there’s a firefighter somewhere who goes over it in his head at three in the morning, asking whether he could have been ten minutes faster, a street closer, a hose longer.

The Mayor came back from across the ocean on the second day. There was a press conference. There were a great many press conferences. The Mayor stood at a podium and said the right things with a face that looked as if it hadn’t slept either. The Governor stood at another podium in another city and said other right things, and also said that somebody should look into the reservoir. Then somebody at the Mayor’s podium said the water system was fine and it was simply overwhelmed. Then somebody at the Governor’s podium said it wasn’t fine at all. The two of them, it became clear over the next few weeks, had discovered that the fire was the other one’s fault. I watched some of this on a television in a school gym where they’d set up a command post, the room where the people running the fight sit with their maps and their radios, eating a sandwich somebody’s grandmother had made, and I thought, they’re fighting it the same way we are. They’re choosing which house to let go.
On the television, in the corner of the screen, there was a little box that said CONTAINMENT: 0%.
It said that for a long time.

Then, very slowly, day by day, the number crept up. Eight per cent. Eleven. Seventeen. Every morning the incident commander stood up in front of the cameras and read out the new number, and every morning the number was higher, and every morning the people who’d lost their houses watched it on hotel televisions and felt nothing, because what did it mean? Contained means the fire won’t get out of the line you’ve drawn around it. It doesn’t mean the houses inside the line come back.

On the fourth night I slept for six hours on a cot in the gym with my boots on. When I woke up it was dark and quiet and the men around me were snoring, and I lay there looking at the ceiling, and I said out loud, to nobody, “Bad idea.”
The probationer, on the next cot, said, “What, Cap?”
“Nothing,” I said. “Go back to sleep.”
He didn’t. Neither did I.
15. The Offer Omid

At 11:40 that night, in the hotel room in Santa Monica, while Tara slept in her clothes and my wife sat in the bathroom with the door closed, crying where she thought we couldn’t hear, my phone buzzed with a text message from a number I didn’t know.

I opened it because I thought it might be a neighbour. It might have been anyone. A lot of people were texting a lot of people that night, checking who had got out, who had a room, who had seen whose house.
It said:

Mr. Kamali, I’m so sorry about what’s happening up there. Terrible day. I know this isn’t the moment, but I wanted you to know my buyers remain very interested in your property, whatever its condition. All cash, as is, quick close. Please keep my number.
It was signed with a first name. The same first name that was on the card in my kitchen drawer, the one with no company on it and a line of small grey print underneath that I’d never read.

I read the message three times. I looked at the time it was sent. I opened the camera app and looked at CAM 3, which had been dead for almost four hours, the last frozen frame still sitting there: the crooked view of the black hill and the orange sky.
The house was still burning when he wrote to me. It may have been burning when he started typing. It was certainly burning when he decided that this was the right night.

I didn’t reply. I sat on the edge of the bed in the dark with the phone in my hand and a feeling I didn’t have a word for then and don’t have a good one for now. It wasn’t anger. Anger would have been simpler. It was the feeling of a man in a room who suddenly understands that the room has another door, and that someone has been standing on the other side of it for a long time, listening.
Things change up here, he had said, in July. On my doorstep. With his good watch.

I want to be careful here. I’ve been careful ever since. I have no proof of anything, and I’m going to say that more than once. A man who buys land for a living sends a text to a man whose land has just become cheaper. That’s not a crime. That’s his job. People have been buying burned land in California for as long as there’s been land in California and fire to burn it. My own father bought his hill cheap from a man who was afraid of a fire. I know that. I’ve thought about that more than I’d like.

But I sat there in the dark, and I thought about the letter from the insurance company in the spring, and the letters in the other mailboxes, all arriving together like birds leaving a tree. I thought about the man at the door in July. I thought about a fire that everybody said had been out. I thought about a reservoir the size of a lake with nothing in it. I thought about a firefighter standing in my driveway looking up at my camera with a hose going limp in his hands.
I didn’t think anyone had planned it. I want to say that clearly. I’m a sound engineer, not a lunatic.

What I thought was worse, in a way. I thought that nobody had to plan it. I thought that a great many people, each doing his own reasonable job — the insurance man reading his risk tables, the land man reading the market, the chief looking after the protected plants, the city waiting on a contract to fix a tear in a cover — had each made one sensible small decision, and that all of their sensible small decisions had added up, like pennies in a jar, to a burned town. And that some of the people who had made those decisions were going to do very well out of it, and none of them were going to be sorry, because none of them, alone, had done anything at all.
At some point my mother spoke from the chair in the dark. I thought she was asleep.
“Who is it?” she said.
“Nobody,” I said. “A man who wants to buy the house.”

She was quiet for a while. Then she said, in Persian, the saying of her grandmother’s from Kashan, the one about the house of glass and the stove. And then, in English, as if she were continuing a conversation she had been having with someone else for a very long time:
“Your father told one of them no. The first time.”
I didn’t know what she meant. I didn’t ask. It was nearly midnight and my house was gone and I didn’t have room in me for one more thing.
I put the phone face down on the bed. After a while the screen lit up again, under the covers, glowing faintly through the white sheet, and I didn’t turn it over to see who it was.
Heard in the Streets
You think I came for your houses like an army. I did not. I came like rain.

I want you to understand how a house burns, because nearly all of you have it wrong, and it matters. You picture a wall of flame marching down a street and swallowing each house whole. Sometimes. Mostly, no. Mostly I arrive as a shower of sparks, the size of your fingernail, riding the wind a long way ahead of me.

They are called embers, and they are the whole of my trick. They land in the gutters full of dry leaves that you have been meaning to clean. They blow in through the little vents under your roof, which you put there so your house can breathe. They settle into the doormat, the stack of firewood against the wall, the dry bark mulch you spread around the roses because it looked tidy. They find the one gap in the one board. Then the house catches from the inside, quietly, while you stand across the street watching the hills, and by the time you see me in the windows I have been living in your attic for twenty minutes.

Then one house gives me the next. That is the other part you forget. I do not need your hills once I am in your streets. Your houses are close together and full of things that burn, and each one I take throws heat and sparks on its neighbour. I walk from roof to roof. I have been doing it in your cities for a long time.

In 1993, in the autumn, I came down the canyon at Topanga, one valley west of where I am speaking now, and I walked all the way to the ocean at Malibu. Three hundred and eighty-eight buildings. Three people. A few days before, I was in Laguna Beach, down the coast, and took more than four hundred homes there. You wrote reports after that too. The reports said: clean your gutters, cover your vents with fine mesh, keep a ring of bare ground around your walls, do not plant oily trees against your windows, build roofs that do not catch. The reports were very good. I have read over their shoulders. Most of you did some of it for a while.
I want to tell you what I found when I reached the high neighbourhood this time.
I found gutters full of leaves. I found bark mulch against the walls. I found pines against the windows, planted by people who loved them.
And I found your water.

Let me be fair, because I have promised to be. Your water was never meant for me. The pipes in those hills were built to fill glasses and bathtubs and a swimming pool on a Sunday, and to put out a kitchen fire or two on a bad night, and they did that faithfully for sixty years. They were not built for a whole town burning at once with every hydrant open and every broken house bleeding water out of its melted pipes into the ground. No town’s pipes are. When the big tanks at the top drained, the hydrants went soft, and the men stood holding empty hoses. That is simply true, and some careful people have said so in a report, and I believe them.
And I will also tell you what I noticed, because I am a witness.

Up a canyon above the neighbourhood there is a great bowl in the ground, built to hold a lake of water for exactly the kind of day this was. When I passed it, I looked in. There was no lake. There was a torn black skin stretched across the bottom of an empty bowl, the cover that is supposed to float on the water to keep it clean, lying there on the dry concrete like a dead thing. It had been lying there for most of a year, waiting on paperwork.

The careful people say it would not have saved you. Perhaps it would not. Perhaps it would have saved one street for an hour. I do not know. I only know that I came expecting water there, and found a skin.

I noticed other things, while I was in the streets. I noticed a man in a driveway looking up into a camera, holding a hose that had gone quiet in his hands, his lips moving. I noticed the old woman’s piano, and I am sorry about the piano; it was the most beautiful thing I ate that day, and it sang a little when I touched it, a long low note from inside, and then stopped.
And I noticed that while I was still in that house, still in the walls and the floor and the piano, a telephone in a hotel room far away lit up with a message about buying the land it stood on.
I was still burning. The land was still hot. I want that written down too.

I do not know what men intend. I have said so, and I will say it again. I only know that some of you were waiting for me, and some of you were waiting for what I would leave behind, and I could not always tell which was which.
IV. ASH
16. The Lobby Omid
For three weeks we lived in the hotel, and so did everybody else.

You’d come down to the lobby in the morning for the free coffee and there they’d be, the whole Palisades, in borrowed clothes. The dentist from two doors down. The family with the two little boys from the white SUV on Palisades Drive, who’d got out and walked, and who turned out to live four streets over. The retired film producer, in a tracksuit that was clearly somebody’s grandson’s, carrying his Oscar in a plastic grocery bag, because it was the only thing he had taken, and he took it everywhere now, into the breakfast room, into the elevator, like a man carrying an urn. People who had lived three streets apart for twenty years and never spoken now sat together on the lobby sofas all day, holding paper cups, telling each other what they’d lost in lists.

Everybody made lists. The insurance people told you to. You sat down with a pad of hotel notepaper and tried to write down everything you had owned, room by room, and you discovered, very quickly, that you could not remember what was in your own kitchen drawers. I got to the drawer with the takeout menus and the dead batteries and stopped, because the card was in there, and I didn’t know how to put that on a list.

The city around us kept going, which was the strangest part. Twenty minutes south, people were at work and at the gym and complaining about traffic. The hotel had a wedding one Saturday. A real wedding, in the ballroom, with a band. We could hear it from the room, the bass through the floor, a cover band playing a song about dancing in September, and the Palisades people in the lobby sat very still and pretended not to hear it, and the wedding people in their good clothes walked past us to the elevators and pretended not to see us, and everybody did a very good job.

The price of everything went up. Hotel rooms, rentals, a two-bedroom apartment in Santa Monica that had been available at one price on Tuesday was available at twice that on Thursday. There’s a law against that in a declared emergency, it turned out, and the Governor said so on television, loudly, and some people were fined, and the prices mostly stayed where they were anyway, because there were ten thousand families looking for somewhere to sleep and not ten thousand places. The National Guard was on the roads. There was a curfew in the burned areas, to stop looters, and there were looters, a few, and they were caught, some of them, dressed as firefighters, which I still can’t think about without a kind of awe at the nerve of it.
And there was the talk.

It started in the lobby on the second day and it never stopped. It went round and round the sofas like the wedding band’s song. Everyone had heard something. Everyone had a cousin who knew somebody. The fire was set on purpose, by a homeless man, by a teenager, by a man with a grudge. It was the power lines. It was the fireworks. The fire department had run out of water because the Mayor had cut the budget. The Mayor had been in Africa. The Governor had let the reservoir go dry. The Governor had sent the water to the fish. There were no fire trucks because they were all at the Olympics. There was going to be an Olympics and they needed the land. The rich had been burned out so that the richer could buy in.

And some of it was worse than that. A man in a golf shirt at the breakfast buffet told a table of us, with great seriousness, that he had seen a video proving the fire was started by a beam from a satellite, and that you could tell because some houses had burned and the trees beside them hadn’t, and because the cars had melted in a funny way, and because the blue things had survived. I didn’t know what the blue things were. He explained that the government was using a laser that couldn’t burn anything blue, and that was why a house with a blue roof was still standing, and he showed us a picture on his phone of a house with a blue roof, still standing.

Tara listened to this with a face I’d never seen on her, a face of pure, clinical interest, like a biologist watching a new kind of insect. When the man had gone to get more eggs she leaned over and said to me, quietly, “Dad. That’s not how any of that works.”
“No,” I said.
“But some of the other stuff,” she said. “Some of it’s kind of true, isn’t it.”

That afternoon she took the pad of hotel notepaper and a pack of sticky notes she’d bought at the pharmacy downstairs, and she began to build something on the long mirror over the dresser in our room. By the end of the week it covered the whole mirror and part of the wall.
17. Seventeen Per Cent Ray
A fire this size doesn’t end. It gets tired.

We worked it for three weeks. Not me the whole time — nobody works a fire for three weeks without sleep, though some of the men tried — but in shifts, twenty-four on and twenty-four off, then forty-eight, then whatever the schedule said that week. It moved north, into the mountains, away from the houses, and a different kind of fight began up there, a slow, slogging, ugly fight on steep ground. We cut line, which means scraping a strip of hillside down to bare dirt so the fire has nothing to cross. We burned out, which means setting small fires on purpose inside that line to eat the brush before the big fire can. And we walked the black. Men came from all over the country. Men came from other countries. There were crews from Mexico and Canada in the same camp, eating the same bad eggs. That was a good thing to see. I want it on the record that there was a good thing.
Every morning, the number. Seventeen per cent contained. Twenty-two. Thirty-one.

I kept thinking about that number. It’s a real measurement, it’s not nothing — it means how much of the fire’s edge has a line around it that we trust. But on the television it had become something else. People watched it like a thermometer on a sick child. Thirty-one per cent. They’d say it to each other in the grocery store. It’s at thirty-one. As if when it reached a hundred, something would be over.
I’ll tell you what a hundred per cent means. It means the edge is held. That’s all. The inside of it is still there. All of it. Every street.

On the ninth day I was in the command post, at the long tables in the school gym where the maps were, when the chief came through. My chief. The one from the ridge, in the clean jacket. He’d been in the command post the whole time, doing whatever chiefs do, which I’m not being sarcastic about; somebody has to hold the phone. He came past my table with two other men and a clipboard, and he looked at me, and I looked at him, and he looked away. Not quickly. Slowly, the way a man looks away from something on a road he doesn’t want to have seen.

We never spoke about it. Not once, in all the weeks after. I know a lot of the other men knew, because men talk, and firefighters talk more than most. There were texts going round within days. Remember the Lachman. Remember the hot spots. The probationer showed me one on his phone, from somebody I didn’t know, at a station across the city. Heard they left it smoking. That’s how it gets out. Not in a report. In a text between two tired men at three in the morning.

The department’s official line, when anybody asked, which the newspapers were beginning to do, was that whatever might have been under that hill had been undetectable. That was the word. Undetectable.
I thought about that word a great deal.
I thought about my hand over the ground. I thought about the rock the size of a loaf of bread. I thought about the thin grey thread coming up out of the crack beside the stump.
I thought: it was detectable. I detected it. I detected it with my hand, which is free, and with my mouth, which said five words, and then I rolled up the hose.

A reporter caught me once, in the parking lot of the command post, a young woman with a microphone and a cameraman behind her. She asked me if I’d worked the New Year’s fire. I said I’d worked a lot of fires. She asked me if the New Year’s fire had been fully put out. I said the department had released a statement about that. She said, “I’m not asking the department, I’m asking you.”
I said, “I’m sorry, ma’am. I’ve got to go.”
She looked at me for a long moment. She was about the probationer’s age. Then she lowered the microphone and said, not to the camera, just to me: “Okay. But somebody should.”
She was right. I got in my truck.

The number crept up. Forty-nine per cent. Sixty. Seventy-seven. Some rain came, a little, at the end of January, the first rain in nine months, too late to matter and just in time to turn the ash on the hills into a grey slurry that ran down into the streets.
On the last day of the month the incident commander stood up and said the magic number. A hundred per cent. Contained.

Everybody clapped. I clapped. We were so tired. And that night on the television, over the pictures of the burned streets, the little box in the corner of the screen said CONTAINMENT: 100%, and I sat in my apartment in Sherman Oaks and looked at it and laughed out loud, alone, for a long time, until it wasn’t laughing anymore.
Contained. Mostly.
18. The Adjuster Omid
Here is what I learned about the FAIR Plan, in the hotel room, over three weeks, on hold.

I learned that when a whole town burns in a single day, everybody calls the insurance company at once, and the insurance company, which is a building full of people in an office park somewhere, discovers what the fire department discovered, which is that there are not enough of them. I learned the hold music, which was classical, and which was, I swear to God, a Chopin nocturne, played badly, on a synthesiser, on a loop. My mother heard it once over my shoulder and said, “She’s rushing,” and went back to her chair.

I learned the ceiling. We had known about it, my wife and I, at the kitchen table in the summer, as a number on a piece of paper. Now it was a number with a house on the other side of it. The FAIR Plan would pay up to its limit to rebuild, and not a dollar more, no matter what it would actually cost to rebuild a steel-and-glass house on a hillside in a town where ten thousand other people were also trying to hire the same contractors. The second policy we’d bought, to fill in the holes, filled in some of the holes. The difference between what we’d get and what we’d lost was a number I wrote down on the hotel notepad and then tore off and folded in half, so I wouldn’t have to look at it.

We were lucky. I want to say that. We could pay for the hotel. We had the other apartment on the east side, rented to strangers, whom we’d have to ask to leave, which is its own small cruelty. There were people in that lobby who’d been dropped by their insurance company in the summer and hadn’t been able to afford the FAIR Plan at all, and had nothing. There were retired people living on pensions in houses they’d bought in 1972, worth millions on paper and not a penny in the bank. The dentist’s wife said to me by the coffee machine, very calmly, “We’re house-rich and cash-dead,” and laughed, and then walked out into the parking lot and stood there for a long time.

The adjuster, when I finally got one, was a kind, exhausted man working out of his car. He’d driven in from Arizona. He had forty-one claims, he told me, just in the Highlands, and more in Altadena, and he hadn’t been home in two weeks. He told me what I’d need: photographs of everything, receipts for everything, a list of everything. He asked if I had photographs of the inside of the house from before.
I said I had security cameras.
“That’s something,” he said. “Most people don’t have anything. You’d be amazed. People don’t photograph their own lives.”

Within the week, the Governor signed an order saying that nobody could make an offer nobody had asked for, to buy land in the burned areas for less than it was worth, for three months. Somebody had noticed. Somebody had been getting texts. The lobby cheered when it came on the television. The next morning I realised the man with the good watch had stopped texting me.
I told Tara. She wrote it on a sticky note and put it on the mirror.

By then the mirror was something to see. She’d put the house in the middle — a sticky note that said HOUSE, with a drawing of it, the steel and glass, surprisingly good — and around it, in a circle, everything else. INSURANCE LETTERS (SPRING). THE MAN W/ THE WATCH (JULY). NEW YEAR’S FIRE (SAME SPOT!!). SMOKE (JAN 4 — “STEAM”). She’d put that one near the middle. She didn’t look at me when she did it. RESERVOIR (EMPTY). HYDRANTS (SOFT). NO EXTRA ENGINES. MAYOR (AFRICA). GOVERNOR (TV). TEXT (WHILE BURNING). ORDER (NO LOWBALLING) → TEXTS STOP.
She’d connected them with lines drawn in the hotel’s ballpoint pen, straight onto the mirror, which I’d have to explain at checkout.
In a separate corner, far from the others, she’d made a smaller circle, labelled NONSENSE, and in it she’d put LASERS and BLUE ROOFS and OLYMPICS and a sticky note that just said THE EGG MAN.
“You’re sorting them,” I said.

“Some of these are things that happened,” she said. “Some of these are things people made up because the things that happened aren’t a good enough story.” She tapped the big circle. “These happened. I checked. The reservoir really was empty. Those texts really came. The insurance companies really left.” She tapped the smaller circle. “These didn’t. People want a villain. Somebody with a laser. It’s easier.”
“And the big one?” I said. “What does it add up to?”
She stood back and looked at it for a long time, her arms folded, sixteen years old, in a borrowed sweatshirt, in a hotel room, in front of a mirror full of her own handwriting.
“I don’t know,” she said. “That’s the scary part. I think maybe it doesn’t add up to anybody. I think maybe it just adds up.”
I’ve never heard it put better. I’ve heard lawyers try.

Because there were lawyers by then. Of course there were. A group of families from the Palisades and from Altadena had got together with a firm downtown, and there was a meeting on a video call that I sat in on, from the hotel bed, with forty other small squares of forty other hotel rooms. The lawyer explained that they were going to sue the insurance companies. They were going to argue that the big companies had not simply decided, each one alone, to stop covering the hills — that they had done it together, all at the same time, like a flock, so that everybody would be pushed onto the FAIR Plan, which the companies themselves were required to pay into and which charged more for less. He said there was a word for companies agreeing together to do something that hurts their customers, and that the word was illegal.
Somebody asked him if he could prove it.
He smiled the way lawyers smile. He said that was what the courts were for.
Afterwards I went and stood in front of Tara’s mirror and found the note that said INSURANCE LETTERS (SPRING), and under it, in small letters, she’d written: everyone’s at once. why?
19. What Everybody Knows Ray
After a big fire, everybody becomes a fire expert. I’ve been through it before. This time it was worse, because this time there were telephones.

I’d come home from a shift and sit on the couch and look at my phone and there it would be, the whole internet, explaining my job to me. There were videos. There were videos of videos. There was a man with a very clean kitchen and a whiteboard who explained, for forty minutes, how the fires had been set by a secret government weapon. His proof was that some houses had burned to the ground while the trees in their front yards were still green, and a fire couldn’t do that, he said, unless it was a laser.
I’ll tell you what I would have told him, if he’d asked me instead of the whiteboard.

A house doesn’t burn from the trees. It burns from the embers. A green tree is full of water and it doesn’t catch easily. A house is full of dry wood and curtains and couches and paper and plastic, and all it needs is one ember in one attic vent. So yes, you’ll find a house burned to its foundations next to a green tree. I’ve seen it a hundred times. It’s not a laser. It’s a house.

He said the cars had melted in a strange way, with puddles of shining metal under them. That’s aluminium. It melts at a much lower temperature than steel. Engine blocks, wheels. Any fire hot enough to burn a house is hot enough to melt the aluminium wheels off a car parked next to it.

He said the blue things had survived. I actually looked into that one, because a guy at the station asked. Some blue things survived. Some blue things didn’t. Nobody posts a video of the blue house that burned.

It’s easy to laugh at those people. The young guys at the station laughed at them. I didn’t, much, because I understood them. A man loses his house to something enormous and stupid and nobody’s fault, and his mind can’t hold it, so it builds something it can hold: a villain with a machine. A villain is a comfort. A villain means somebody could be stopped.
The trouble was, there were other things too. Quieter things. Things I couldn’t laugh at, because I’d been there.
I knew about the hoses on the ridge.
I knew there’d been no extra engines sent to the Palisades on the night of the wind, when in other years there had been.
I knew the shift had gone home.
I knew about the engines in the yard with their wheels off, because I’d stood there in December and been offered one for Christmas.
I knew, now, like everybody, that the reservoir had been empty.

And I was starting to hear, in the way you hear things in the department, that people were already writing the report. There’s always a report after a big fire. It’s called an after-action report, and it’s supposed to be the department looking at itself in the mirror and writing down honestly what went right and what went wrong, so it can do better next time. The man writing it was a good man, a battalion chief, one rank above a captain like me, whom I’d known for years, careful and honest, and I heard he was writing it straight. And then I heard that other people were reading his drafts. And then I heard that some of the sentences were coming out. The sentence about the engines. The sentence about the shift. The sentence about the ridge.
I heard it the way you hear about a rock slide on a road you haven’t driven yet.

Somewhere in there, in the weeks after, the Mayor fired the chief of the whole department. Not my chief — the big one, at the top. There was a press conference. The reason given was the thing about the shift, about not holding over the men and not sending the engines. Some people said it was right. Some people said the chief was being thrown off the sled so the wolves would slow down. The chief said that the budget had been cut and there hadn’t been enough of anything. The Mayor said the budget hadn’t been cut that much. They both had numbers. Everybody always has numbers.

I sat in my apartment and watched it and thought about my own chief, on the ridge, in the clean jacket, saying the same sentence twice. Nobody fired him. Nobody even knew his name. And I thought about me, rolling the hose, and nobody knew my name either.
That’s the thing about a disaster made of a thousand small decisions. You can fire one person at the top of it, and everybody feels better, and the other nine hundred and ninety-nine go back to work.
The probationer came by one evening with a six-pack. We sat on my little balcony overlooking the parking lot and drank it and didn’t say much. After a while he said, “Cap, can I ask you something?”
“Sure.”
“If we’d stayed. On the ridge. If we’d kept digging. Would it have mattered?”

I thought about lying to him. It would have been kind. He was going to be a firefighter for thirty years, and he was going to carry that question up and down a lot of hills, and I could have taken it off him with one word.
“I don’t know,” I said. “Maybe not. Maybe there were ten more of them under that hill and we’d have found one. Maybe the wind would have found another. Maybe it would have come from somewhere else.”
He nodded.

“But it would have been the right thing to do,” I said. “That part I do know. It would have been the thing the job is for. And we didn’t do it. I didn’t. I was the captain and I said it was a bad idea and then I did it anyway, because a man in a clean jacket said it twice.”
He was quiet for a long time.
“You said it, though,” he said. “You said it was a bad idea. I heard you.”
“Yeah,” I said. “Put that on my headstone. He said it was a bad idea.”
He laughed. I laughed. It was a terrible joke. We drank the rest of the beer.
20. The Chimney Omid
They let us back in at the end of the month, with an escort, for a few hours, in white suits.

That’s the first thing nobody tells you. You don’t just drive home. The ash is poison. Everything that burned — the paint, the plastic, the batteries, the car tyres, the pool chemicals, the pesticides under every kitchen sink in the neighbourhood — all of it is now a fine grey powder that gets into your lungs and your skin, and before anyone can so much as pick through the rubble, men from the federal government in white hazardous-material suits have to go through every lot and take away the worst of it. Then the Army Corps of Engineers comes, with trucks, to scrape the lots bare. For the first visit, they gave us white paper suits of our own, and masks, and gloves, and told us not to touch anything we didn’t have to, and not to stay long.

We went through a checkpoint at the bottom of Palisades Drive. There were soldiers there, National Guard, young men and women with rifles who looked like they’d rather be anywhere else, checking our driver’s licences against a list. One of them, a girl who couldn’t have been much older than Tara, said to my mother, very gently, “I’m so sorry, ma’am.” My mother patted her hand.
Then we drove up.

I want to describe it, and I can’t. I’ve been trying for a long time. I make sounds for a living and I have no sound for it. The best I can do is this: it was quiet. That was the thing. The whole way up the canyon, the whole length of Palisades Drive, the whole of the Highlands, there was no sound. No birds. No sprinklers. No leaf blowers. No dogs. No televisions through open windows. No wind, even; the wind had gone back to the desert where it lives. Just the engine of our car and our own breathing inside the masks.

And grey. Everything grey. Street after street of grey, in the shapes of houses. You could see the plan of each house laid out on the ground in ash, like a drawing: here was the kitchen, here was the hall, here was where the bedrooms were. And standing up out of every plan, like a gravestone at the head of a grave, the chimney. The brick chimneys were the only thing that didn’t burn. Whole streets of them, in rows, standing alone, black at the top, pointing at the sky.
We parked at the bottom of our driveway. Tara got out first. My wife stayed in the car. My mother and I walked up together, holding hands like children, in our white paper suits.
My father’s house was a frame.

The steel had held. I want to say that for him. The glass was gone and the floors were gone and the roof was gone and everything inside was gone, but the steel frame was still standing on the hill, twisted in places, sagging in one corner where the heat had been worst, but standing, like the skeleton of some enormous animal that had died on its feet. You could look straight through it to the ocean. The column by the stairs, the one he knocked on twice every morning, was still there.
The pool was full, and perfectly blue, and the only thing on the whole hill with a colour.

And at the back, where the living room had been, where the glass wall had sagged and broken while I watched it on a hotel bed, there was a strange shape lying in the ash. It was big and dark and curved, and at first I didn’t know what it was. It looked like a harp. Like a great iron harp lying on its side, the strings gone, just the frame.
My mother knew. She walked straight to it.
“The piano,” she said.

It’s made of iron, the inside of a grand piano. I didn’t know that. The wood burns — the case, the keys, the lid, the legs — and the strings snap and melt, but inside every grand piano there is a heavy iron plate, shaped like a harp, which holds all the tension of all the strings, and it doesn’t burn. It just lies there when everything else is gone, like a bone.
My mother knelt down beside it in her white paper suit. She put her gloved hand on the iron, very gently, the way she used to put her hand on a child’s shoulder when they were rushing.

She didn’t cry. I’ve never seen my mother cry. She stayed there a long time, kneeling, with her hand on it. Then she stood up and brushed the ash off her knees, and looked around at the whole grey hill, and said something to herself in Persian, too quiet for me to hear.
Tara was up at the back of the lot, near where the pine trees had been, where the slope started going up toward the ridge. She called me.
“Dad. Look.”

At the edge of the lot, in the grey ash, among the black stumps of my father’s pines, something was growing. A few big soft leaves, grey-green, pushing up out of the ash from an old root that had survived underground. Just leaves. No flower yet.
My mother came and stood beside us and looked at it for a long time.
“Tātureh,” she said.
“It’s already growing back,” Tara said. “How is anything growing back?”
“It likes it,” my mother said. “It likes the ash. It likes it when everything else is gone.” She looked up the hill, at the black ridge. “It’ll flower in the summer. The way it’s supposed to.”

I didn’t say anything. I was looking up at the ridge too, at the place near the top of the trail where the New Year’s fire had been. There were little coloured flags stuck in the ground up there. Dozens of them, orange and blue and yellow, in a pattern. I asked one of the escorts what they were. He said the investigators had put them there. The federal ones. They were marking where the fire had started.

He pointed. It was the same spot. Exactly the same spot. The place where the black patch had been. The place where Tara and I had stood on the fourth of January and watched a thread of grey smoke come up out of the ground and decided it was steam.
On the way back down the driveway, my mother stopped by the steel column at the bottom of the stairs, the one that was still standing. She reached out and knocked on it. Twice.
“A hundred years,” she said. “He said a hundred years.” She looked at me. “It stood forty-five. That’s a good house, Omid-jān [oh-MEED-jaan]. That’s a very good house.”
It was the first time since I was a small boy that she’d called me that.
21. Declared Out Ray
A week after they called it contained, I drove up to the ridge on my day off and walked up the trail alone.

I don’t entirely know why. I told myself I wanted to see the flags. The investigators had been up there for weeks, the federal ones, with their cameras and their little coloured markers and their notebooks, working out where it had started. Everybody at the station knew what they’d found. It was going to be in the newspapers soon. A holdover, they were going to call it. A fire that had held over from the one before — that had lain in the ground for six days and come back. That’s the official word. Holdover. It’s the same word we use for keeping a shift on duty after it’s supposed to go home.
I thought about that on the way up. We didn’t hold the shift over. The fire did.

The hill was black. All of it, from the top of the trail to the bottom of the canyon and beyond, as far as you could see in every direction, black and grey and silent. The stumps of the old brush stuck up out of the ash like the bristles of a burned broom, just the way they had on the second of January, only now it was everything, the whole mountain, not eight acres. It was very quiet. My boots made a soft crunching sound in the ash, and that was the only sound there was.
The flags were where I knew they’d be.

I stood in the middle of them. The patch of stumps near the top. The old chaparral with the thick woody bases, fifty years old or more. I found the rock. I swear to you I found the same rock, the size of a loaf of bread, grey, sitting just where it had sat. I took my glove off and put my bare hand flat on it.
Cold. Stone cold.
That’s what it feels like, when a fire’s really out. You’d think it would be a relief.

I stood there a long time with my hand on the rock. I thought about a lot of things. I thought about my father’s hands shaking when he held a cup, and the one time he told me about 1961, sitting on the porch of our house in the Valley when I was about fifteen and had just said I wanted to join the department. He’d told me about the wooden roofs catching from the top down, and the embers riding ahead, and standing in a street in Bel Air with a hose and watching houses catch that he hadn’t reached yet. And then he’d said something I’d forgotten until that morning on the ridge.
He’d said, The fire always tells you where it’s going. Nobody ever wants to hear it.

Near the rock, in the ash, something was coming up out of the ground. A few big grey-green leaves. I knew what it was. Every firefighter in those hills knows what it is. It comes up after fire. It likes the ash.
I crouched down and looked at it.
“You were watching,” I said to it. Out loud. On a mountain. To a weed. “The whole time.”
It didn’t say anything. It’s a plant.

I stood up and put my glove back on. I looked down the canyon toward the Highlands, toward the grey streets with the chimneys standing in rows, and I found the one I was looking for without really trying. You could see it from up there. A steel frame on a steep lot, a skeleton on a hill with the ocean showing through its ribs, and next to it a swimming pool, perfectly blue, like somebody had left a piece of the sky lying on the ground.
The house with the cameras. The one where I’d looked up.

I don’t know who lived there. I never found out. I’d thought about it, in the weeks since. I’d thought about finding out, driving up there, knocking on the door of whatever apartment they were in now, and saying — what? I’m the one who stood in your driveway. I’m the one whose hose went soft. I’m the one who rolled the hose on the ridge. I said it was a bad idea.
Put that on my headstone.
I walked back down the trail. At the bottom, at the truck, I looked back up at the ridge once more, the way you look back at a house when you leave it.

On the radio, on the way home, a woman read the news. She said the Palisades fire had been declared contained. She said the investigation into its cause was ongoing. She said the department had said that any fire remaining underground after the New Year’s blaze would have been undetectable.
I turned the radio off.
The clock on the dashboard said 12:12.
Heard in the Ash
Six years before this, in the autumn of 2018, I was in two places on the same day.

In the north, in a town in the pines called Paradise, I took almost everything. Eighty-five people. Nearly fourteen thousand homes. I came through that town so fast that people died in their cars on the one road out, which I want you to remember, because you have a great many towns with one road out. The same morning, down here, I came over the hills at Woolsey, near the valley, and walked all the way to the ocean at Malibu again, the way I had in 1993, and took more than sixteen hundred buildings on the way.
That was the year the insurers did their arithmetic.

I will explain it plainly, because it is not complicated, only dull, and the dull things are the ones that ruin you. An insurance company is a bet. You pay it a little every year, and it bets that your house will not burn. It makes that bet with ten thousand families, and most of the houses do not burn, and the little payments from all of them add up to more than the few houses it has to rebuild, and the difference is its living. It works beautifully, as long as the houses keep mostly not burning.

In 2017 and 2018 the houses burned. More of them than the bet allowed for. The insurers paid out, by their own accounts, more in two years than they had taken in for many years before. And they looked at their tables, and they looked at the hills, and they looked at me, and they concluded that I was going to keep coming. They were right. I will give them that. They understood me better than your cities did.

So they wanted to charge more. And your state has rules about how much an insurer may charge and how it may decide — old rules, written by voters in another century, to protect people from companies who charged too much. Under those rules, raising the price was slow, and hard, and argued over for years. So the companies did the other thing. They stopped selling. One after another, they stopped writing new policies in the hills. Then they stopped renewing old ones. The letters went out. The families were pushed, one by one, into the lifeboat — the plan of last resort, the one the companies themselves are required to pay into, which charges more for less.

Now. Some families say it was not one after another. Some families say it was all at once, together, by arrangement, and they have gone to court to say so, and a judge has said they may make their case. I do not know if they are right. I was not in the room. I only noticed that the letters arrived in the high neighbourhood in the same season, in the same envelopes, like birds leaving a tree all at once — and that birds leaving a tree all at once can mean a hawk is coming, or can mean that one bird moved and the others followed. You cannot tell from the ground.
I noticed also that when I had finished, and the ash was still warm, men came to buy the land.

Not all at once. Quietly. Some of them were families who had lost their own house and wanted to stay near their neighbours. Some of them were builders, who have always bought burned land, and always will. And some of them were people with a great deal of money and no faces, who sent texts in the night and offers by telephone, cash, as is, quick close, to people who were sitting in hotel rooms counting the difference between what they had and what they had lost. By the end of that year, of the burned lots that sold in the high neighbourhood, roughly two in every five went to people who buy land to sell again. The Governor made a rule for a while that nobody could offer less than the land was worth. For a while.

I want to be very careful, because I have promised to be. I am not telling you that anyone called me. I cannot see into a boardroom. I am telling you that a great many people, in a great many rooms, each made a sensible small decision, and each decision left a door open for me, and when I came through the door there were other people standing on the far side of it, already holding a pen.
Some of you think that is a conspiracy. Some of you think it is just a market.
I have been burning longer than either word has existed. From where I stand, I cannot see the difference. I am not sure there is one.
Heard at the Edge
I am going to tell you something now that I have not told anyone.
I have been here before.

Not in 1961. Not in 1993. Not in any of the years I have already told you about. I mean here. This ridge. This night. These white flowers, open when they should be closed. This small bright mark on the hill, just after midnight, while the fireworks are still going up over the city.

I remember it the way you remember a room you have stood in once: every detail sharp, and none of it quite in the right order. I remember the wind that is coming. I remember the soft hoses and the black skin in the empty bowl and the iron harp lying in the ash. I remember a man with his hand on a cold rock. I remember a girl in front of a mirror, drawing lines.
Fire has no calendar. I have told you that. I burn in all my years at once. Sometimes I cannot tell whether a night has already happened or has only been waiting.
Listen.
Somewhere below me, in a station at the bottom of the canyon, a man is sitting very still in a chair with a plate on his knees.
Somewhere below me, on a deck behind a glass house, a man is sitting beside his mother under a blanket, with a telephone in his hand.
The white flowers are open. They have been open all night. They are very sweet.
In a moment, a clock is going to say something.
V. CONTAINED, MOSTLY
22. Twelve Twelve Ray
I was rinsing my plate at the sink when the tones dropped.
No.
That isn’t right. I have to tell this part exactly, or none of the rest is worth anything.

I wasn’t at the sink. I was in the recliner in the day room, the brown one with the broken footrest that nobody will let us throw away. There was a paper plate on my knee with half a piece of bad cake on it, and the plastic fork had fallen on the floor. On the television, with the sound down, New York was showing the ball drop again, three hours late, for the West Coast, a crowd of people in plastic hats. Two of the guys were asleep on the couch. The probationer was in the kitchen doorway with his jacket half on, looking at me.
And the tones were going. Loud. Real. The sound every firefighter knows in his spine.
Brush fire. Reported by callers. Near the top of the trail above the Highlands.

I didn’t move. That’s the first thing I remember. For maybe two seconds, which is a very long time when the tones have dropped, I sat in that chair with the plate on my knee and did not move at all, because I did not know what year it was.

I knew it was the first of January. I knew that the way you know your own name. But I also knew — I knew it with my whole body, the way you know a bone is broken — that it was February, and that I had just come down off a black mountain with my hand cold from a rock, and that a steel house was standing like a skeleton on a hill with a blue pool beside it, and that the whole of the Palisades was ash, and twelve people were dead, and the chief of the department had been fired, and a report was being written with the true sentences taken out of it. I had lived all of that. I had lived it for weeks. I could feel the weeks in my legs.
The microwave in the kitchen said 12:12.
“Cap?” the probationer said. “Cap, you coming?”
I got up. The plate fell off my knee. I went to the engine. My body did it without me, the way it’s done it for twenty-seven years. On the way, through the open bay door, I looked up at the ridge.

There it was. A little orange glow, high up, near the top of the trail. Small. Pretty, almost. Like a campfire somebody had left. All around it, on the dark slope, dozens of small pale shapes that I knew were flowers, white, open, turned toward us.
I stopped in the middle of the bay floor and the probationer walked into my back.
“Sorry, Cap.”
“What day is it?” I said.
He looked at me strangely. “New Year’s,” he said. “It’s New Year’s. It’s, like, twelve minutes into New Year’s.”
I want to tell you what I felt, and I can’t do it in a straight line, so I’m going to do it the way it came.
I felt sick. Actually sick, a hot wave up from my stomach into my throat.

I felt relief so large I almost sat down on the concrete. Nothing had happened yet. Nobody was dead. The houses were there, all of them, lit up for the holidays down the canyon, every window, every Christmas light. The steel house was there. I didn’t know where it was, exactly, but I knew it was there, somewhere in those lights, with its glass wall and its cameras and a piano in the living room I’d never seen.
I felt like a man who has been let out of prison and told that he hasn’t been sentenced yet.
And then I felt the worst thing, which was that I knew what the next two hours would look like, and the next six days, and I was right.

We went up the trail road in the dark, with the engine grinding in low gear, and the fire sat on the crest like a necklace somebody had dropped. It was eight acres. I knew it would be. There was no wind. I knew there wouldn’t be. We ran the hose up the trail, and the helicopter came in low with its big light on, like a lighthouse that had decided to go for a walk, and dropped its water, and the water came down silver through the searchlight and hissed where it landed.
The probationer said holy shit, softly, reverently, like he was in church.
I said it with him. The same two words, at the same time. He turned and looked at me with his mouth open. I didn’t explain. What would I have said?

By four in the morning we had a line around it. By sunrise it was contained. The incident commander got on the radio and said so, in the exact words I had heard him use, in the exact tone, and every man on that hill breathed out at once, except me.

I stood on the ridge with the sun coming up over the city and the ocean going from black to grey to silver, and the smoke from the little burned patch lying down flat and drifting away east, and I said to myself, very quietly, the only word I had for it.
Dream.

It was a dream. That’s what it had to be. I had fallen asleep in a recliner with a plate of cake on my knee at twenty to twelve on New Year’s Eve, after standing out behind the station smelling something sweet coming down off the hill, and I had dreamed for half an hour, and in that half hour I had lived five weeks.

I had never in my life had a dream like it. I don’t have dreams, much. I’m a firefighter; I sleep like a dropped sandbag. When I do dream, it’s the ordinary kind, the kind where you’re late for something and your teeth fall out. It isn’t the kind with weather in it. It isn’t the kind where you can smell the ash on your own gloves, and read the numbers on the clock, and feel the particular weight of a hose that has gone soft.

I didn’t tell anyone. Not that morning. Who do you tell? Chief, I had a dream. I could hear how that would sound. I could hear exactly how that would sound, because I’ve been in this job long enough to have laughed at men who said less.
So I did what firefighters do with things they can’t say. I went back to the station and ate eggs and didn’t say it.

But I’ll tell you what I did before I left the ridge. I walked over to the patch of stumps near the top. The old chaparral with the thick woody bases, fifty years old. I found the rock, grey, the size of a loaf of bread, right where it was going to be.
I took off my glove and put my bare hand on it.
It was warm.
23. Sāl-e No Omid
I woke up because my phone was buzzing in my hand.

That’s all. That’s the whole of it. I was sitting in a deck chair on the back deck of my father’s house with a blanket over my knees and an empty wine glass on the boards beside me, and my phone was buzzing in my hand, and I opened my eyes.

The screen showed a photograph. Tara, in a paper crown, pulling a face, at my wife’s family’s party with the coat check. The message under it said happy new year from the fancy people xx. It had been sent at 12:01.
The time on the screen said 12:12.

I don’t know how long I sat there. I remember the sounds first, because sounds are my job. The fireworks. Pop-pop-pop, thinning out now, over the village, over the flats of Santa Monica, over the Valley behind the hills. A dog barking somewhere down the canyon. The small tick of the house settling behind me in the cold, the steel frame contracting a little the way it always does at night. My mother breathing, beside me, in the other deck chair. She was asleep under her blanket, in her good coat, with her chin on her chest, snoring very gently, the way she has snored my whole life and denied it my whole life.
Then I looked up at the ridge, and it was on fire.
Not much. A small bright orange mark, high up, near the top of the trail, right in the middle of the white flowers. Like somebody had struck a match in the back row of a theatre.
I made a sound. I don’t know what sound. My mother woke up.

She didn’t say anything at first. She lifted her head the way deer lift their heads, and she looked at me, and then she followed my eyes up the hill to the little orange mark, and she looked at that for a long time. Then she looked back at me.

I have spent my whole life reading my mother’s face, and it has always been like reading a letter in a language I only half speak. That night I read it all the way to the bottom. There was no surprise in it. There was something like pity, and something like tiredness, and something else I didn’t have a name for until much later, which was recognition. The recognition of one person who has come back from somewhere, seeing that another person has come back from the same place.
“We’ve done this before,” she said.
“Maman,” I said. “Maman, the house—“
“I know,” she said. “It’s here. Go and look.”
I went and looked.

I got up out of the deck chair with the blanket falling off me and went through the sliding door into the house, and it was all there. All of it. The glass wall, whole, black, reflecting the room and me in it with my mouth open. The living room. The rug. The big grey sofa. The Steinway, with its lid down, and my mother’s reading glasses on top of the lid where she always leaves them. The kitchen. The clocks on the oven and the microwave and the coffee machine, all saying the right time, not blinking, just quietly telling the truth.
I put my hands flat on the glass wall. It was cold. It was solid. It didn’t bend.
I went to the column at the bottom of the stairs, the steel one, and I knocked on it twice.

Then I went to the kitchen drawer, the one with the takeout menus and the dead batteries, and opened it, and there was the card. A name. A phone number. No company. A line of small grey print underneath.
I read the grey print. For the first time. Under a kitchen light at a quarter past twelve on New Year’s night, in my socks, with my heart going like a trapped bird.
It was the name of a company. Just a name. Something bland, with Holdings at the end of it, and an address in an office building downtown.
It wasn’t proof of anything. It was a business card. I put it back in the drawer. I closed the drawer.

Then I went back into the living room and sat down at my mother’s piano, which I have not played seriously since I was twelve years old, and I lifted the lid, and I pressed one key. A low one. I held it down and let it ring.
It rang for a long time in the dark house. I sat and listened to it until there was nothing left of it at all.

When I went back out onto the deck, my mother was standing at the railing with the blanket around her shoulders, watching the ridge. The fire engines were up there now. You could see their lights moving along the trail, red and white, very small, and the long beam of a helicopter searchlight coming in low over the crest, and under it, falling, a curtain of water, silver in the light.
“They’ll put it out,” I said. “Tonight. It’ll be out by morning.”
“Yes,” she said.
“And then it’ll come back.”
She didn’t answer that. She didn’t have to.

We stood there together until the sky started to go grey over the city. I didn’t say anything else and neither did she. At about six, when the helicopter had gone and the lights on the ridge had thinned out to one or two, she turned to go inside, and she stopped at the door, and put her hand on my arm.
“When you’re ready,” she said, “I want to show you something. Of your father’s. No.” She corrected herself. “Of mine.”
24. Two Hours and One Hose Ray
On the morning of January second we walked the black.

It was all the same. That’s what I want you to understand. The cold. The grey powder. The stumps sticking up like the bristles of a burnt broom. The ground warm like a bed somebody had just got out of. The probationer working his patch near the top with his glove off, and looking up at me with that strange expression, and saying, “Cap. It’s hot.”
I was already beside him. I’d walked to that patch first thing, without meaning to.

We started digging. And about twenty minutes later, the chief came up the trail in his clean jacket, with his radio on his hip, and the look on his face of a man who had been on the phone since six o’clock with people who do not walk hillsides.

I have thought about what I did next more than I have thought about anything in my life, including my marriage. I want to tell it plainly and not make it bigger than it was, because it wasn’t big. It was the size of a conversation on a hill.
He told us to pack it up. Roll the hose. We were done here.
I told him about the hot ground. I told him about the rock.
He told me about the protected plants. The parkland. The people who look after the park not wanting us tearing up the hill. The fire was out. Crews had been over it all night.
And I said the five words. “Chief, this is a bad idea.”

I watched his mouth. I knew what he was going to say. He was going to say it again, in the same tone, the way orders get said the second time. And I knew that when he’d said it twice, twenty-seven years of this job were going to bend my back down and pick up that hose for me.
So I didn’t wait for the second time. I kept talking. I’d had a whole month to work out what I’d say, and I said it.
I said, “Chief, give me two hours and one hose. That’s all. We’ll stay off the plants. We’ll dig the stumps that are hot and nothing else. Two hours.”
He started to say something. I kept going.
I said, “And I want a drone up here. One of ours, with a thermal camera. I want to fly the whole burn and see what’s hot. Then if it’s clean, we leave, and I’ll roll the hose myself.”

The department has drones, you see. It had them the whole time. Small ones, with cameras that see heat instead of light, so a patch of ground that’s hotter than it should be shows up on the screen glowing white. They’re used for exactly this. They’re just not always used, because somebody has to ask for one, and asking for one means saying out loud that you think the fire might not be out, and nobody likes to be the man who says that at the end of a long night when everybody wants to go home.
I said it. On the radio, too, not just to his face. I got on the radio and asked for the drone, which meant it was said in a place where it would be written down.

He looked at me for a long time. I’d known him fifteen years. He’s not a bad man. I want to keep saying that, because it matters. He wasn’t a villain. He was a tired man in a clean jacket in the middle of a system that rewards the fire being out and punishes the fire not being out, and he’d been told that morning, by somebody above him, that the fire was out, and I was making him say it wasn’t.
“Two hours,” he said finally. “And stay off the plants.”

The drone came up a little before noon. A young technician drove it up the trail road in a pickup and flew it off the tailgate, a little buzzing thing no bigger than a dinner plate, and we all crowded round the screen on his lap to watch.

On the screen, the burn scar was a grey ghost of the hillside, all in shades of grey, cold ground dark and warmer ground lighter. And scattered across it, in the patch of old stumps near the top, and in a few other places further along, were small white spots. Glowing. Like stars on a cloudy night.
The technician counted them. He got to eleven and stopped counting out loud.
Nobody said anything. The chief was standing behind me, looking over my shoulder at the screen. I felt him go still.
After a while he said, quietly, “Keep the line on it.”

That’s all. Keep the line on it. He turned around and walked back down the trail, and got on his phone, and I don’t know who he called or what he told them. He didn’t say anything else to me that day. He didn’t say anything else to me for a week. And that fire was not declared out on January second.

We dug for two days. We dug up the stumps, one by one, the old woody ones that had been growing on that ridge since before the probationer’s parents were born, and we opened them up, and inside some of them — not all of them, some of them — we found it. The thing I’d told the probationer about in the first year. A coal the size of your thumb, lying in a tunnel the width of a pencil, down in the root, glowing orange, patient, eating very slowly. We found five of them. Five. We spread them out and drowned them and turned the dirt over and drowned it again.
On the evening of the third, the drone flew again, and the screen was grey all over, with no white spots anywhere.
The fire was declared out.
Declared out. The two most expensive words in the job.

I didn’t believe them. I want to be honest. I’d found five. The drone said there were none left. And I’d learned that month — that month which hadn’t happened, which I had lived anyway — that a thing can be undetectable and still be there. There might have been a sixth. There might have been one the camera couldn’t see, too deep, under a rock. The ridge is big, and the roots go down a long way, and I was one man with a shovel and a dream.
So I did the only thing left. I went back.

On the evening of the fourth, and again on the fifth, on my own time, I drove up the trail road after dark and walked the burn alone with a flashlight and my bare hand. I didn’t find anything. The ground was cold. The rock was cold.
The white flowers were still open, all the way up the slope, all around me, very sweet, turned toward me in the dark. I stood among them with my flashlight and didn’t look at them too long.
25. The Notebook Omid
My mother showed me the notebook on the afternoon of New Year’s Day, at the kitchen table, while my wife and Tara slept off the party upstairs.

I had told her everything by then. It took most of the morning. I told her about the smoke and the soft hydrants and the six cameras going dark, about the hotel and the lobby and the man with the Oscar in a grocery bag, about the white suits and the grey streets and the iron harp in the ash. She listened without interrupting, which she has never done in my life. When I got to the piano she closed her eyes. When I got to the part where she knelt beside it and put her hand on the iron, she opened them again, and nodded, very slightly, as if I had confirmed a date.
Then she went to my father’s study and came back with a small notebook. Old, brown leather, the corners worn round. I’d never seen it before. She put it on the table between us.
“Nineteen eighty,” she said. “The first night in this house.”

She opened it. The pages were covered in her handwriting, in Persian, small and neat, the ink gone brown with age. I can speak Persian, badly. I can’t read it well. She read it to me, translating as she went, running her finger along the lines from right to left.

It was a dream. She had written it down in the morning, the first morning they woke up in the new house, when the paint was still wet and there were no curtains and the whole canyon was full of sunlight. She’d dreamed that night, she wrote, of white flowers on the hill above the house, open in the winter when they should have been closed. Of a wind so dry it made her hands crack. Of the glass wall, my father’s glass wall, bending inward in the middle like a sheet of plastic in an oven. Of her piano, lying in grey ash, nothing left of it but its iron heart, like a harp on its side. And of a boy.
“A boy,” she read, “grown, with a face like his father’s, sitting in a small room far away, watching our house burn through a little window in his hand.”
She stopped reading. She put her finger on the line and kept it there.

“I didn’t have a little window in my hand in 1980,” she said. “Nobody did. I didn’t know what it meant. I thought it was a television. I thought it meant a son who would watch television too much.” She almost smiled. “That part came true too.”
I couldn’t speak.

“I told your father,” she said. “At breakfast. The first morning. I told him the whole thing.” She shrugged, the Persian shrug, with the whole face. “He laughed. He said, Āzar, you’re afraid of a little fire, like the American. The man who sold us the lot. He was very proud of that joke. He told it for forty years.”
“You stayed,” I said.

“We stayed.” She closed the notebook and laid her hand flat on the cover. “What were we going to do? We’d left one country already. We had nothing to go back to. We had this house and his job and you, two years old, asleep upstairs. And I thought: it’s a dream. My grandmother’s flowers. It means nothing.” She looked up the hill through the glass, at the ridge, at the black patch and the white flowers and a single fire engine still parked at the end of the trail road, small in the afternoon light. “And every year, after that, I watched the flowers. Every summer they opened, the way they’re supposed to, and every winter they closed, and I thought, good. Forty-four years. Every winter, closed.” She was quiet for a moment. “Until this one.”
“Maman. When did they open? This year?”
“Christmas,” she said. “I noticed at Christmas. I’ve been standing at that window for a week.”
The tidying. The albums stacked on the desk beside the empty bag. The back doors she’d stopped opening. It smells like August.
“Why didn’t you tell me?” I said.
She looked at me with something very tired and very kind.

“Would you have listened?” she said. “Your father didn’t. And you are more his son than mine.” She put her hand on mine. “Now you’ve seen it yourself. That’s different. Nobody listens to someone else’s dream. You have to have your own.”
There was one more thing, and she told it to me before the others came down. She told it quickly, looking at the notebook and not at me, the way you tell something you’ve kept too long.
“The man with the watch,” she said. “The one who came in the summer. You put his card in the drawer.”
“Yes.”

“A man came before. In 2018. After the big fire in Malibu, the one on the television. A different man, same kind of card. Same kind of watch. He said he represented buyers. He said things change up here.” She shrugged. “Your father told him no. He said the house would stand a hundred years. The man said, Of course, of course, and smiled, and left the card, and your father threw it away.” She looked up at me. “I didn’t. I kept it. It’s in the back of this book.”

She opened the notebook at the back cover and there it was, tucked into a pocket in the leather. A business card. A different name. The same bland kind of company, with Holdings at the end of it, and the same office building downtown.

“It doesn’t mean anything,” my mother said. “I know. People buy land. People have always bought land. Your father bought this land from a frightened man.” She slid the card back into the pocket. “But they’ve been coming up the hill for a long time, Omid-jān. Waiting. Like the flowers.”
26. The Driveway Omid
On the afternoon of January second, I went up the trail to find him.

I didn’t know his name. I didn’t know which station he was at. I only knew his face, from a small square on a small screen, black with soot, squinting up into a camera for three seconds. And I knew that the fire crews would be up on the ridge that day, walking the black, because in the dream they had been, and the dream had been right about everything.

Tara came with me. I hadn’t told her anything. I’d said I wanted to see what a fire left behind, and she’d looked at me the way my mother looks at me and said, “That’s usually my line,” and put on her good shoes.
