They were there. A crew of five, near the top, in the patch of old stumps, digging. A fire engine at the end of the trail road with its hoses run up the hill. A young man sitting on the tailgate of a pickup with a little drone on his knees. And in the middle of it, leaning on a shovel, taking a break, with his helmet off and his grey hair plastered flat with sweat, a man in his fifties with a face I’d have known anywhere.
I walked up to him. He watched me come. He had the look firefighters get when civilians walk into their work, polite and wary. Tara stayed a few steps behind me.
I didn’t know how to start. I’d been rehearsing it all the way up the trail and none of it was any good. So I just said it.
“You stood in my driveway.”
He looked at me. He didn’t say anything.

“On the seventh,” I said. “In the afternoon. Around three. A steel house with a glass wall, at the top of the Highlands. There was a hydrant at the curb and it went soft on you, and you walked back to check it, and you looked up. At the camera over the garage. You looked straight up into it.”
His face didn’t change at all. That was what told me. A man who doesn’t know what you’re talking about frowns, or smiles, or asks. His face just stopped, like a clock.
“You said something,” I said. “I couldn’t hear it. There was too much noise. But your lips moved. You were looking right at me and your lips moved.”
The probationer, the young one, had stopped digging and was staring at us. Tara had come up beside me.
The firefighter set his shovel down against a stump, very carefully, as if it were made of glass.
“I said I’m sorry,” he said.
His voice was hoarse. He cleared his throat.
“I didn’t say it out loud,” he said. “I thought it. I thought it at the camera. Somebody’s going to see this. I’m sorry.”
“Yes,” I said.

We stood there on the burned ridge looking at each other for a long time. The wind was very light. It was cold. Below us, down the canyon, my father’s house stood on its hill with its glass wall catching the afternoon sun, whole.
“Your pine trees,” he said at last. “On the side of the house. They went up like torches.”
“My father planted them,” I said. “When I was a baby.”

“You said there was a piano,” he said. “I never saw it. I saw the frame. After. From up here. A steel frame on a steep lot, and a blue pool. I stood up here in February with my hand on a rock and I looked down at your house.” He stopped. “I thought about finding you. I didn’t know who you were.”
“My mother says it stood forty-five years,” I said. “She says that’s a good house.”
He almost laughed. It came out of him like a cough.
Tara was looking from one of us to the other. “What,” she said, very slowly, “is going on.”

So we told her. We sat on two burned stumps on the ridge, the firefighter and me, with the crew digging around us and the probationer pretending not to listen and the young man with the drone definitely listening, and we told her, in pieces, interrupting each other, finishing each other’s sentences. The clocks at 12:12. The white flowers. The hoses rolled on the second of January. The soft hydrants. The hotel. The report with the sentences taken out. We compared it like two men comparing directions they’d been given to the same house: did you go left at the church? Yes. And then the gas station? Yes, the one with the broken sign. It matched. Everything he’d seen, I’d heard about. Everything I’d seen, he’d been somewhere near. Some of it neither of us had seen, only known, the way you know things in dreams.
Tara listened to the whole thing with her clinical face. The biologist watching a new kind of insect. When we got to the hotel room and the mirror, she went quiet.
“The mirror,” she said.
“You covered it in sticky notes,” I said. “With lines drawn between them in hotel pen. You had a separate corner for the nonsense. You called a man at breakfast the egg man.”
She looked at me for a long moment.
“That sounds like me,” she said, in a small voice. “That’s the scariest thing you’ve said.”
Then she said, because she’s her grandmother’s granddaughter: “Okay. So how?”

The firefighter looked up the slope at the white flowers. We all did. They were open in the afternoon, which they shouldn’t have been either — they close in the day — all the way up the trail, dozens of them, pale and still.
“Momoy [MO-moy],” he said.
“What?”

“That’s what the Chumash called it. The people who lived here before. A park ranger told me years ago. They used it — the old ones, the ones who knew how — to see things. Things that were far away. Things that were coming. It’s dangerous. It’ll kill you, if you don’t know what you’re doing. It’s full of things that’ll make you see what isn’t there.” He shook his head. “But you’d have to eat it. Drink it. Not smell it from a deck.”
“We smelled it,” I said. “Both of us. New Year’s Eve. Before midnight. It came down off the ridge.”

“I know,” he said. “I smelled it too. I stood out behind the station trying to place it.” He was quiet. “The smell shouldn’t do anything. I’m telling you that honestly. I’ve read the reports. I’ve taken people to the emergency room who ate the seeds. You don’t get anything off the smell but a headache.”
“And yet,” Tara said.
“And yet,” he agreed.
My mother’s grandmother’s word, in Kashan. The thieves used it to take your rug. The saints used it to see.
We sat with that for a while. Then the firefighter said the thing that I’ve come to think is the truest thing either of us said that day, and maybe the truest thing in this whole account.
“Here’s what gets me,” he said. “It doesn’t matter how we saw it. Not really. Because there wasn’t anything in it that was a secret.”
I looked at him.

“Think about it,” he said. “Every piece of it was lying around in plain sight. The brush that hadn’t burned in fifty years — you could see it from the road. The wind — the weather service said it was coming, in words they almost never use. The engines in the yard — I stood there and looked at them before Christmas. The reservoir — it was empty for a year, it was on a city website somewhere. Your insurance leaving — you had a letter. The man with the watch — he gave you his card. And the fire on this hill, under these stumps —“ He knocked the side of his boot against the one he was sitting on. “I put my hand on it. I felt it.”
He looked out over the canyon at the houses.

“Nobody needed a magic flower to see this coming,” he said. “We needed somebody to put all the pieces in one room at the same time. That’s all the dream did. It put them in the same room.” He shrugged. “And then made us live in it for a month so we’d believe it.”
Tara said, very quietly, “That’s what the mirror was.”
27. Six Days Ray

Here is what a fire captain can do in six days, and what he can’t. I’m going to put it down plainly, because I promised myself on that ridge that if I ever got the chance to write it down I wouldn’t make it sound cleverer than it was.

What I did on the ridge. You know that part. Two hours and one hose. The drone with the heat camera. Five coals the size of a thumb, dug out and drowned. Then two more nights on my own with a flashlight and my bare hand. That’s the first lesson and it’s the simplest one: walk the black until it’s cold, then walk it again, and when you have a camera that can see heat, use it every time, not just when somebody’s brave enough to ask. A fire that is “declared out” is a guess with a uniform on. Make the guess with the best tools you’ve got.

What I did with the forecast. On the third, when the weather service first started hinting at the wind, I wrote a memo. Me. A captain. I’d never written a memo in my life that wasn’t about a broken toilet. I wrote it the plain way, one page. I said: a big Santa Ana is forecast for the sixth and seventh. The Palisades has old dry brush, one road out, and a hillside that just burned and may not be cold. In 2011, in a wind like this one, we pre-deployed forty extra engines to the high-risk areas, including this one. I am asking that we do it again. I am asking that the outgoing shift be held over on the sixth. I am asking for water tenders — those are trucks that carry their own water, big tanks on wheels — to be parked and ready in the Highlands before the wind, so that if the hydrants go soft we have something to fight with. I sent it up the chain. Then I sent it sideways, to every captain I knew. Then I called my friend near the top, the one who’d told me respond, and read it to him over the phone.
He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, “Ray, what’s got into you?”
I said, “I had a bad feeling.”
That’s true. I just didn’t say how long the feeling had lasted.

What came of it. Some. Not all. I want to be honest, because a story where one man’s memo saves a city is a lie, and this isn’t that story. On the sixth, three extra engines came to the Palisades. Three, where we’d needed ten or twenty or forty. Some of the shift stayed on, the ones who volunteered, because I’d asked them to, and because in a firehouse, when the captain who never asks for anything asks for something, people listen. Two water tenders were parked at the top of the Highlands, full. It wasn’t a plan. It was a patch. But it was something standing where there had been nothing.

What I couldn’t do. I couldn’t fix the engines in the yard. Nobody can grow mechanics in six days, or conjure the money that should have paid for them over the last five years. Those engines sat there with their wheels off, on the sixth, the same as in the dream.

I couldn’t fill the reservoir. I tried. I actually tried, which made me feel like a fool. I called the water department on the fourth and got a very patient woman who explained that the reservoir had been empty since early last year because of the tear in its cover, and that fixing a cover on a reservoir that size requires a contract, and a contract requires bids, and bids take time, and even if the cover were fixed tomorrow, filling a hundred million gallons into a bowl takes weeks, and the water has to be tested to be safe to drink. She was right about every single thing. I thanked her. I hung up. I sat in my truck and said a word I won’t write down.
And I couldn’t un-grow the brush. That’s the big one. That’s the one that isn’t a six-day problem at all.

What a city could do, if it wanted to. I’m going to put this down too, because a firefighter who’s lived through the thing twice ought to be allowed to say it once. None of it is new. Every one of these is in a report somewhere, written by somebody smarter than me, after some fire, and then put on a shelf.

Burn the hills on purpose, in small pieces, in the cool wet months, with crews standing by, the way the people who lived here first did for thousands of years. Not everywhere, and not too often — chaparral burned too often turns into weeds, and weeds are just a faster fuse. But some. The fire is coming to these hills anyway. It’s always been coming. The only question is whether it comes in small visits we choose, or in one enormous visit that chooses us.

Cut fuel breaks along the ridges, wide strips where the brush is cleared back to low ground so a fire running along the top has somewhere to slow down, and keep them cut, year after year, not just after the last disaster.
Pay for the mechanics. Pay for the reserve engines. It is the most boring line in any budget and it is the one that decides whether there’s a fire engine on your street when you need one.

When the weather service uses the words particularly dangerous, pre-deploy. Every time. Hold the shift over. Every time. Stage water. Every time. Most of those times, nothing will happen, and someone will ask what the overtime was for. The answer is: that’s what it’s for.

Build the houses differently. Metal mesh on the vents so the embers can’t get in. Roofs that don’t catch. Five feet of bare ground around every wall, no mulch, no woodpile, no hedge. No oily trees against the glass. It’s all in the building code for new houses now, more or less. The old houses are the problem, and there are a lot of old houses.
Plan the road out before you need it. One road out of a neighbourhood is a trap, and everybody knows which neighbourhoods have one road out. Plan to empty them early, before the fire, not during.
And when the fire’s over, write the report straight. Leave the true sentences in. The whole point of looking in a mirror is to see what’s actually there.
That’s it. That’s everything I learned in a month that didn’t happen. It fits on a page. It always did.
On the night of the fifth, I went back up to the ridge again. Cold ground. Cold rock. White flowers, open, sweet, turned toward me.
I said to them, out loud, like a fool, “I heard you.”
They didn’t say anything. They’re plants.
28. The Kitchen Table Omid

On the morning of January third I started doing the things you’re supposed to do. I’d known what they were for years. Everybody on the hill knew. There were pamphlets. There were postcards from the fire department in the mailbox every spring. I’d put them in the recycling with the pizza menus.
This is the list. It’s not a clever list. That’s the point of it.

The first five feet. The fire department calls it Zone Zero: the ring of ground right against the walls of the house. Embers land there and find something to burn and then the house catches from the bottom. So you make it bare. It took me till dark. I raked out every inch of the bark mulch my father had spread around the walls because he liked how tidy it looked. I moved the woodpile off the side of the house and down to the bottom of the lot. I pulled out the dry hedge under the kitchen window. I took the cushions off the deck furniture and put them in the garage. I took the doormat in. It sounds like nothing. It took me a whole day, and my back hurt for a week.
The trees. The two pine trees on the side of the house. The ones my father planted when I was a baby. The ones that exploded on CAM 4.

I couldn’t cut them down myself. On the afternoon of the third I was standing in the street looking at them, trying to work out who I could call at no notice in a week when every tree person in Los Angeles was on holiday, when a pickup truck went past with rakes and mowers in the back, slowed down, and stopped.

It was him. The young man from Palisades Drive. The one who’d pulled out of a driveway into the burning canyon and said get in, get in, and driven us down the wrong side of the road with his hazard lights going.
He didn’t know me, of course. He’d never met me. He was just a landscaper doing his rounds, who’d slowed down because he saw a man staring at his own trees the way people do before they call someone.
“You need help with those?” he said.
“Yes,” I said. I couldn’t say anything else for a moment. “Yes. Please.”

He and his cousin took them down the next morning. It took them six hours. When they’d finished I paid him more than he asked, and he tried to give some of it back, and I wouldn’t take it. Then I asked him his name. He told me. I wrote it down. I’ve kept it.

I’m not going to put it here. It’s his. But I know it now, and in the other version I never did, and of all the things that changed in those six days, that’s one of the ones I’m proudest of, and it’s the smallest.
The gutters. Full of pine needles. I got on a ladder and cleaned them out by hand. I found a tennis ball from 1991 up there.

The vents. There are little vents all round the bottom of the roof, so the attic can breathe. Embers get in through them. You can cover them with a very fine metal mesh, so fine a spark can’t get through. I bought every roll of it at the hardware store in Santa Monica and spent a day on the ladder with a staple gun. I didn’t finish. I did most of them.

The pictures. On the fourth I went through the whole house with my phone and filmed it. Every room. Every drawer. Every shelf. Inside every closet. I talked while I filmed, like a tour guide, saying what everything was and when we’d bought it. The adjuster in the dream had said people don’t photograph their own lives. I photographed mine. It took three hours and it was one of the strangest afternoons I’ve ever spent, walking through my own house describing it to a stranger who might never need to see it.

The papers. Passports, birth certificates, the deed, the insurance policies, the hard drives with twenty years of my work on them. My mother’s notebook. The photograph albums, forty-five years of them, the ones from Tehran and the ones from here. All of it into two plastic boxes, and the boxes into the back of the car, and the car parked facing down the hill.

The insurance. My wife and I sat at the kitchen table on the fourth and read the FAIR Plan policy, all of it, every page, which I don’t think anyone in the history of the world has ever done. We found the ceiling. We found the gaps. We called our agent, at home, on a Saturday, and I think the fact that we’d read the policy frightened him more than anything we said. We raised what we could raise. We added what we could add. It still didn’t reach the number on the other side. It got closer.

The road out. On the fifth, I walked down Palisades Drive with Tara. The whole way, from our house to Sunset. It took us well over an hour on foot. We counted the side streets. We found the two places where a road cuts through to another neighbourhood, which I hadn’t known were there after a lifetime of living at the top of that road. We agreed, out loud, standing on the corner of Sunset, that if we ever had to leave, we’d leave early, before anybody told us to, and if the road jammed we’d get out and walk and not wait.
“Dad,” Tara said, on the walk back up. “You know we’re doing the whole list from the pamphlet.”
“I know.”
“The pamphlet that comes every year.”
“I know.”
“Why didn’t we just do it before?”

I didn’t have an answer that wasn’t embarrassing. Because it was a pamphlet. Because the house was steel. Because it hadn’t burned in forty-five years. Because I’m a man who makes fake fire sound real for a living and never once thought about the real kind. Because a piece of paper in a mailbox is not the same as watching your mother kneel in the ash.
“Because nobody listens to someone else’s dream,” I said. “You have to have your own.”
She looked at me sideways, the way she does when she’s deciding whether I’ve said something intelligent by accident. Then she let it go.

The neighbours. I told some of them. Not about the dream; about the brush, the wind, the fire on the ridge that might not be out. I told the dentist. I told the family with the two little boys. I told the film producer at the top of the road, who listened to me politely, holding a cup of coffee, and then told me that he had lived in these hills for thirty-one years and had seen a great many wind events and that the fire department was very good, and did I know that he had once won an Academy Award, and I said yes, I knew, my father had held it.
The family with the two little boys cleared their gutters. The dentist moved his woodpile. The producer did nothing. I think about that. You can’t make someone else have your dream.
The man with the watch. On the evening of the fifth, I took his card out of the kitchen drawer and called the number.

He answered on the second ring. Warm voice. He remembered me. Of course he did. He said how nice it was to hear from me, and how sorry he’d been about my father, and was I thinking about the conversation we’d had in the summer?
“I wanted to ask you something,” I said. “Why now? Why did you come in July?”
There was a very small pause. Not long. The length of a man deciding which true thing to say.

“Things change up here,” he said pleasantly. “That’s all. The market changes. Insurance is getting difficult for people on the hill. Some families find it’s a good moment to think about what they want.”
“And if the house burned down,” I said. “Would your buyers still be interested?”
Another small pause.
“My buyers are interested in the land, Mr. Kamali,” he said. “The land is always there.”
I thanked him. I told him I’d think about it. I hung up. I put the card in my mother’s notebook, in the pocket at the back, next to the other one from 2018.

The kitchen table. That night, the fifth, we sat down at the kitchen table, all four of us. My wife, my mother, my daughter, me. Three generations of the family in the glass house, at the same table my father had eaten breakfast at for forty-four years, knocking on the steel column on his way past.
My wife asked the question, because somebody had to. “Do we sell?”

We talked about it for a long time. My wife was for selling. She’d never loved the house the way I did; it was my father’s, and my mother’s, and in some way it had never quite been hers. Tara was against. She said it was the best view at school and she’d only just got it. I didn’t know. I said so. I said I’d watched it burn and I’d watched it stand and I didn’t know which one was true.
My mother listened to all of it with her hands folded on the brown notebook.
Then she said: “We leave on the sixth. In the evening, before the wind. All of us. We go to a hotel. We take the albums and the papers. We don’t wait to be told.”
Nobody argued. It wasn’t a suggestion.
“And afterward?” my wife said.

“If the house is here in February,” my mother said, “we sell it. In the spring. To a family. Not to him.” She tapped the notebook where the cards were. “Not to anyone with a watch like that. To a family who wants to live here and knows what they’re buying. We tell them about the brush. We tell them about the wind. We give them the pamphlet.” She paused. “We tell them about the flowers.”
“And if it isn’t here?” I said. “In February?”
My mother looked out through the glass wall, up the dark hill, at the ridge where the white flowers were still open.
“Then it stood forty-five years,” she said. “And it was a good house. And we were in it together.” She put her hand on mine. “We left one country already, Omid-jān. We can leave a hill.”
Nobody said anything for a while. Then Tara said, “Can I at least keep the view until the spring?”

My mother laughed. It was the first time I’d heard her laugh since before my father died. It was a real laugh, loud, the one she used to use in the old days when one of her students played a wrong note so badly it was funny.
“Yes, azizam [aa-zee-ZAM],” she said. “Keep the view.”
29. The Sixth Ray

The wind came at about nine, the way it had before. The long soft roar down the canyon. The bay doors rattling in their tracks. The flag standing straight out from the pole like it had been ironed that way.

There were three extra engines parked in our lot. Three engines from across the city, with crews on them, eating my chili. There were men on cots in the day room who should have gone home at eight that morning. At the top of the Highlands, two water tenders sat at the end of a dead-end street, full, with their crews asleep in the cabs.

It wasn’t enough. I knew it wasn’t enough. If the fire came the way it came before, with the wind throwing embers a mile ahead, into twenty places at once, three engines and two tenders were a few buckets against a flood.
But it was a few buckets more than last time. And the ridge had been walked, and dug, and flown, and walked again.

At about ten I drove up the trail road one last time in my own truck, against every rule in the book, in a wind that tried to push me off it, and I walked out onto the burn with my flashlight. The wind was so strong I had to lean into it to stay standing. The ash was blowing off the ground in grey sheets, stinging my face. The old stumps we’d dug out lay on their sides where we’d left them, their roots in the air like upturned hands.
I took my glove off and put my hand on the rock.
Cold.
I stood there with my hand on it for a long time, in the dark, in the wind, the white flowers trembling all around me, turned toward the houses below.

Cold. It was cold. I told myself that, over and over. It’s cold. And I knew, the whole time I was telling myself, that a rock can be cold and a root under it can be warm, and that a thumb of fire in a pencil of dark can lie very quiet for a very long time, and that I was one man with a flashlight and a bare hand on a very big mountain.
I drove back down. I didn’t go to bed. I sat in the brown recliner in the day room with my boots on, all night, awake, listening to the wind working at the building, finding every seam.
I didn’t eat any cake.
Omid
We left at six in the evening, before the wind. All four of us, and the albums, and the papers, and my mother’s notebook, in two cars.

My mother walked through the house before we left. Every room. Slowly. She touched things — the back of the sofa, the kitchen counter, the frame of Tara’s door. At the piano she stopped and lifted the lid and played something. Not a whole piece. A few bars. A nocturne. The one she used to hum on the deck. She played it very slowly, the way she always told her students to play it, not rushing.
Then she closed the lid and put her reading glasses on top of it, where she always leaves them, and walked out through the front door, and didn’t look back.
At the bottom of the driveway I stopped the car and looked back at the house, because you do.

The hotel was in Santa Monica, four blocks from the beach. The same hotel. I’d booked it on the second of January, the day I came down from the ridge, and they’d given me a room at the ordinary price, because nobody else had booked yet, because there was no reason to. It was a small room with two beds and a window that looked out on the back of another hotel.
At nine the wind came. We heard it even in Santa Monica, a long roar coming down from the hills, and the palm trees in the street outside bending over like old men.
At eleven I opened the camera app.
Six windows. Six little squares. My house.
CAM 1, the front gate. Dark. The plants thrashing in the wind.
CAM 2, the driveway. Empty. The hydrant at the curb, just a shape.

CAM 3, the back deck, looking up the hill. The deck furniture without its cushions. The railing. And above it, the dark ridge, black against the orange glow of the city lights on the clouds, and nothing on it. No glow. No spark.
CAM 4, the side yard. Two stumps where the pines had been, and bare earth.
CAM 5, the garage. My father’s workbench. The Christmas decorations in their box.
CAM 6, the living room, looking out through the big glass wall. The sofa. The rug. The Steinway with its lid down and my mother’s reading glasses on top.
At about a quarter past eleven, as I watched, the picture in CAM 6 flickered. The lights in the living room went out and came back on. A power flicker, up on the hill, in the wind.

And reflected in the dark glass of the wall, faint, like a ghost of the room behind the camera, I could just see them. The clocks. The microwave and the oven. Blinking. The way they do after an outage, when they’ve lost their minds and have to be told again what time it is.

My mother was sitting in the chair behind me with the albums on her knees. She’d seen it over my shoulder. She didn’t say anything. She reached out and put her hand on my back, between my shoulder blades, the way she used to when I was a boy and couldn’t sleep.

I didn’t sleep. I sat on the edge of the hotel bed all night with my phone in my hand, watching six small squares of my house, while the wind came down off the mountain and the palm trees bent over in the street, and somewhere in the dark above the Palisades a ridge full of white flowers waited, very sweet, for the morning.
30. Ten Twenty-Nine Ray
Seven o’clock. Grey light. The wind is worse than the night. A palm frond as long as a canoe comes down across the station’s driveway and lies there like a dead thing.

I take one of the extra engines up to the top of the Highlands. I don’t ask. I park it in the driveway of the steel house, the one with the glass wall and the cameras. I’ve never been here in daylight in this version. The house is beautiful. I didn’t know that. The last time I stood here, the pines were about to go.
The hydrant at the curb is there. I have a man check it. Good pressure. For now.
Nine o’clock. The sky is going the colour of a dirty nickel.

Ten o’clock. The wind is trying to take the engine off the hill. We stand in its shelter and watch the ridge. My probationer beside me. He’s got his glove off already, the way I taught him. I don’t know what he thinks he’s going to feel from here.
I look up at the camera over the garage. The little glass eye. I don’t know if anyone’s watching. I lift my hand, a small wave, like a fool.
“Cap,” he says. “What are we waiting for?”
“Nothing,” I say. “Hopefully nothing.”
Omid
Ten o’clock. Santa Monica. The hotel room. My wife and Tara asleep, finally, on one bed. My mother in the chair, awake, the albums on her knees.
On my phone, in a small square, CAM 2. A fire engine in my driveway. A man in yellow, grey-haired, standing by the hydrant, looking up into the camera. He lifts his hand. A small wave.
I wave back, at the phone, in a hotel room eight miles away. He can’t see me. It doesn’t matter.

CAM 3. The back deck. Looking up the hill. The ridge, black against a brown sky. The dug-out stumps near the top, their roots in the air. And all along the trail, on either side of it, the white flowers.
They’re still open. In the morning. In the wind. In January.
Ray
Ten twenty.
Ten twenty-five.

The wind drops for a second, the way it does sometimes, a breath held between gusts, and in the silence I can hear everything. The engine idling. The probationer’s breathing. A dog barking somewhere down the canyon. The dry brush on the hillside moving against itself, a sound like somebody slowly crumpling cellophane.
I look up at the ridge.
Omid
My mother puts her hand on my back, between my shoulder blades.
On CAM 3, in the small white numbers in the corner of the window, the camera is keeping time.
The wind comes back.
31. The Way It’s Supposed To Omid
I woke up because my phone was buzzing in my hand.
That’s all. That’s the whole of it, again. I was sitting in a folding chair in the dark with a blanket over my knees, and my phone was buzzing, and I opened my eyes.

It was a text from Tara. where are you guys. it’s 4am. grandma’s not in her bed. The time on the screen said 4:07. Not 12:12. Just 4:07, the ordinary, careless time of a night that has gone on too long.
It was warm. That was the first thing. The air on my face was soft and warm, and full of the sound of crickets, and there was no wind at all.
Then the smell. Sweet. Heavy. Like flowers left too long in a vase.
I looked up.
There was no house.

There was a flat rectangle of bare, scraped dirt where the house had been, raked smooth by the machines in the spring, with little orange survey flags at its corners. There was no steel frame. There was no column by the stairs to knock on. There was no chimney, even; they had taken the chimney too. There was only the swimming pool, empty now, a blue hole in the ground with a skin of dead leaves at the bottom, and beyond it the dark canyon, and beyond that the lights of Santa Monica, and the black line of the sea.
And all around the edge of the lot, and up the slope behind it, and all the way up the black ridge to the top of the trail, the white flowers were open.
Hundreds of them. Big as teacups, pale in the dark, turned toward me. Blooming in the heat, in July, the way they’re supposed to.

My mother was in the other folding chair, beside me, asleep under her own blanket with her chin on her chest. The canvas bag was on her knees. The same bag. The one she’d carried down Palisades Drive on the seventh of January, with forty-five years of photograph albums inside it, while I held her arm and the hills burned on both sides of the road.

We had driven up at eleven the night before, the two of us, with two folding chairs from the trunk of a rented car. It had been her idea. She had said, at dinner, in the rented apartment in Santa Monica, that the flowers would be open now, and that she wanted to see them, and that she wanted to see them from her own land. I had said it was a bad idea. She had looked at me the way she looks at me.
And we had sat down among the flowers in the warm dark, and I had smelled them, and I had fallen asleep.
And I had dreamed that I woke up on New Year’s night with my house still standing.

I sat very still in the folding chair and let it come apart in my hands. The ridge dug out and drowned. Ray’s memo. The three extra engines. The gutters, the vents, the pines coming down, the landscaper’s name written on a card. The kitchen table. We can leave a hill. Six days of doing everything right. All of it had felt like the waking. None of it had happened.
The fire had happened. The fire was the only part that was real.

I didn’t cry. I want to say that I did, because it would make a better story, but I didn’t. I sat there in the warm dark and felt something I didn’t have a name for, and still don’t, a kind of grief that was also, somehow, a kind of relief. As if I had been allowed, for one night, to go back and do it properly, and had been shown exactly how, and then had been handed back to the world as it is.
My mother woke up.
She lifted her head the way deer lift their heads. She looked at the flowers. Then she looked at me.
“Did you get the pines down,” she said. “This time?”
I stared at her.
“Yes,” I said. “A landscaper did. The one from Palisades Drive. I learned his name.”
She nodded slowly, as if I’d told her a train had been on time.
“Good,” she said. “That’s good.”

She opened the canvas bag and took out the brown leather notebook. The one from 1980. The one that had been in the bag on the seventh of January because she had put it there on the morning of the seventh, on top of the albums, without telling anyone. She opened it at the back, where the little leather pocket was, and showed me. Two business cards. One from 2018. One from July of last year, the one I’d put in the kitchen drawer with the dead batteries, which she must have taken out of the drawer and kept.
Then she turned to the last written page.
It was dated January the first, 2025. In her small, neat Persian hand. She read it to me.

The white flowers opened at Christmas. The same as the first night. I told Omid tonight on the deck that we have done this before. He thought I meant New Year’s. Nobody will listen. His father didn’t. I have taken the albums down from the shelves.
She closed the notebook.
“You knew,” I said. “In January. The real January.”
“I dreamed it,” she said. “In 1980. It’s not the same thing as knowing.” She put the notebook back in the bag. “If I had told you, you would have said it was a dream. You would have been right.”

Next door, at the edge of the neighbour’s scraped lot, there was a new sign on two wooden posts. I could just read it in the light from the city. SOLD. And under it, in smaller letters, a name I recognised. The same bland name with Holdings at the end of it. The same office building downtown.
I read it for a long time.

Then a car came up the street in the dark, slowly, with no siren and no lights on top, and stopped at the bottom of what had been our driveway. A pickup truck. A man got out. Grey-haired, in a plain jacket, not a uniform. He stood at the bottom of the drive and looked up at us, two people in folding chairs on a bare lot among the white flowers, my phone still lit in my hand, and he didn’t come any closer.
I knew him. I had never met him. I knew him the way you know a face from a small square on a small screen.
I got up and walked down to him.
We stood there on the pavement where the hydrant still was, the one that had gone soft, with its cap painted fresh yellow.

“I saw your light from the ridge,” he said. “I’ve been sleeping up at the trailhead some nights. I knew which lot it was.” He looked past me, up at the bare ground and the blue hole of the pool. “I stood in your driveway.”
“I know,” I said.
He had something in his hand. A few sheets of paper, folded long. He held them up a little, the way you’d show someone a ticket.

“I wrote it down,” he said. “What I’d do. The engines. The shift. The water. The ridge. I wrote it in the truck, tonight, up at the trailhead. I woke up and I wrote it all down before it went.” He looked at the pages. “I’m sending it up in the morning. To the man writing the report. It’s too late for here.”
“It’s not too late for the next hill,” I said.
“No,” he said. “It’s not.”

We didn’t say anything else for a while. Up the slope, my mother had stood up, with the blanket around her shoulders, and was looking out at the city. Behind her the ridge was black, and covered in white flowers, and above it the sky was beginning, very faintly, to go grey.
I’ve thought a great deal, since that morning, about why I’m writing this down.
I think it’s because of something my mother said, at a kitchen table that doesn’t exist, in a January that never came. Nobody listens to someone else’s dream. You have to have your own.
She’s right. She usually is. I know that you can’t have mine.

But I’ve written it down anyway, as plainly as I can, the whole of it, the fire and the dream and the six days of doing it properly. Because the hills above your house are waiting too. Everyone’s are. And I would like, just this once, to be the one person in the story who was listened to.
Heard in the Summer

It is quiet now. I have gone back into the ground and the roots and the long patience of the brush, and the hills are green again at the bottom, and the white flowers are open in the right season, and I am asleep. I want to say one more thing before I sleep properly, and then I will not speak again for a while.
You spent a great deal of time, after I left, deciding whose fault I was.

I watched you do it. The one in charge of the city and the one in charge of the state stood at their separate podiums and each discovered, with real sincerity, that I was the other one’s fault. The chiefs found that I was the budget’s fault. The budget found that I was the chiefs’ fault. The companies found that I was the risk’s fault, and the risk was a number, and a number cannot be sued. Men wrote a report about me and then other men took the truest sentences out of it, one by one, the way you take the stones out of a fruit, so that it would be easier to swallow.
I want you to know that none of it reached me.

I do not read reports. I do not vote. I have never once been flattered. No one has ever bought me lunch, or given me a title, or promised me a better office if I would only be patient until after the election. I have no friends in high places and no enemies in low ones. I did not come to the high streets because the people there were rich, and I did not spare the house with the tile roof because its owner knew someone. I came because the brush was dry, and the wind was east, and the ground under one old stump was still warm.
That is the whole of my reasoning. It has been the whole of my reasoning for ten thousand years.

You have a thousand ways of deciding what matters. You rank things. You decide that this year the money goes here and not there, that this road gets repaired and not that one, that the mechanics can wait and the reservoir can wait and the small fire on the ridge can be declared out because everybody is tired and wants to go home. You call this priority. You call it politics. You call it the art of the possible. I think it is a very human art, and I do not hold it against you. But I want you to understand that I do not practise it. I have no priorities. I have only conditions. When the conditions are met, I come. When they are not, I sleep.

So when you ask me whether I will come again, I cannot tell you anything a weather report could not. When the brush is old enough. When the rain stops long enough. When the wind comes down the canyons from the desert, the way it always has. I will not check first who is in office. I will not ask who has been warned. I will not care whether you have written anything down.

This is the part that sounds cruel, and it is not. It is the only kindness I have. Because I do not care who you are, I cannot be bribed and I cannot be fooled, and so everything that works against me works for everyone. The cleared ground works for the rich man and the poor man exactly the same. The small fire you set on purpose in the cool months, with somebody watching, takes the same old brush from above the mansion and above the rented room. The water you keep in the high bowl is the same water whichever house it reaches. I am the one thing in your world that cannot be lobbied. You could learn to love me for that.

The old people who lived here first understood this. They did not pray to me and they did not fight me. They simply paid attention, every year, whoever was chief, whatever had happened the year before. They let me in a little at a time, in the right season, with someone watching. They did not need me to be kind. They only needed to be ready.
That is all I have to teach you. I am not your enemy, and I am not your friend, and I am not a judgment on anyone. I am weather with teeth. I am the hills breathing out.

The white flowers are open now, the way they’re supposed to be. The man with the folded pages is sending them up in the morning. The woman with the canvas bag is watching the city wake. Somewhere under this ridge, in a root older than any of your laws, something small and patient is already beginning, very slowly, to grow.
I will be back. I am not threatening you. I am only telling you the truth, the way I always have.
Contained, mostly.
Never out.

GLOSSARY
Āzar [aa-ZAR] — Persian, fire. Omid’s mother’s name.
azizam [aa-zee-ZAM] — Persian, my dear one. An endearment, used to a child or someone loved.
chamise [shuh-MEEZ] — from the Spanish, brushwood. A tough, oily evergreen shrub that covers the dry hills of Southern
California and burns very hot.
chaparral [SHAP-uh-RAL] — from the Spanish, place of scrub oak.
The dense, drought-hardy shrubland of the California hills, which grows for decades between fires and needs fire to renew itself.
Chumash [CHOO-mash] — The Indigenous people of the coast north and west of Los Angeles, from Malibu to San Luis Obispo, who used datura in ceremonies to see what was coming.
datura [duh-TOO-ruh] — from the Hindi, the thorn-apple plant.
Sacred datura, a native Southern California wildflower with large white trumpet flowers that open at night in summer. Every part of it is poisonous.
jān [JAAN] — Persian, soul, life. Added after a name as an endearment, as in Omid-jān.
Kamali [kaa-maa-LEE] — The family name of Parviz, Āzar, Omid and Tara.
Kashan [kaa-SHAAN] — An old desert town in central Iran, known for its carpets and rosewater, where Āzar’s family came from.
Maman [maa-MAAN] — Persian, from the French, mother. What
Omid calls Āzar.
momoy [MO-moy] — Chumash, datura. The Chumash name for the plant and for the drink made from it.
Omid [oh-MEED] — Persian, hope. The narrator’s name.
Parviz [par-VEEZ] — Persian, victorious. Omid’s father, the engineer who built the house.
sāl-e no mobārak [SAAL-eh no mo-baa-RAK] — Persian, blessed new year. The ordinary Persian greeting for the new year.
Santa Ana [SAN-tuh AN-uh] — Spanish, Saint Anne. The hot, very dry wind that pours down from the inland deserts toward the
Southern California coast in autumn and winter.
Tara [TAA-raa] — Persian, star. Omid’s daughter.
Tātureh [taa-too-REH] — Persian, datura. What Āzar calls the white flowers on the ridge.
Tehran [teh-RAAN] — The capital of Iran, where Parviz and Āzar grew up.
Tongva [TONG-vuh] — The Indigenous people of the Los Angeles basin, who lived along its rivers for thousands of years and used small, controlled fires to tend the land.
